Simulated long-term dynamics of Tasmanian devil populations following the introduction of devil facial tumour disease (DFTD). Scenario 1 illustrates disease extirpation, whereas Scenario 2 demonstrates stable coexistence between host and pathogen. Upper panels show changes in devil population size over 100 years of simulation, middle panels present Morlet wavelet power spectra identifying shifts in the strength and periodicity of population cycles through time, and lower panels show the prevalence of DFTD. Together, the simulations demonstrate how epidemiological processes can generate contrasting long-term outcomes ranging from pathogen loss to persistent endemic disease accompanied by characteristic oscillations in host abundance.




Research overview


The study provides a major conceptual advance in wildlife disease ecology by demonstrating that realistic representation of within-host disease progression and individual heterogeneity can fundamentally alter predictions of long-term epidemic outcomes. It challenges conclusions drawn from earlier compartmental models by showing that severe initial population declines do not necessarily imply eventual host extinction, highlighting the importance of distinguishing transient epidemic dynamics from long-term eco- epidemiological processes when forecasting disease impacts and evaluating conservation interventions.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Individual-based epidemiological models that explicitly represent temporal changes in pathogen burden and transmission can predict long-term disease outcomes that differ substantially from predictions produced by homogeneous compartmental models.





Model scenarios calibrated to ten years of empirical Tasmanian devil data predicted that devil facial tumour disease is more likely to fade out locally or persist through long-term coexistence than to drive Tasmanian devil populations to extinction.





Progressive tumour growth creates temporal variation in host mortality and infectiousness that slows epidemic spread and increases the likelihood of long-term host–pathogen coexistence through delayed disease dynamics.





Long-term persistence of devil facial tumour disease is predicted to produce multi-year oscillations in host abundance and disease prevalence rather than stable equilibrium dynamics or inevitable host extinction.





Combining individual-based simulation with approximate Bayesian computation enables estimation of plausible epidemiological parameters and selection of model structures that best reproduce observed host demographic and disease patterns.





Early severe population declines following emergence of devil facial tumour disease should not be interpreted as evidence of inevitable long-term extinction, and intensive management interventions may be unnecessary unless supported by long-term epidemiological forecasts.





Severe population declines observed during the early stages of an emerging infectious disease do not necessarily predict long-term population collapse because transient epidemic dynamics may differ fundamentally from long-term endemic dynamics.





Reliable assessment of disease impacts on wildlife populations requires models that capture long-term eco-epidemiological processes, as conclusions based solely on short-term observations of emerging epidemics can lead to misleading forecasts and inappropriate management decisions.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Emerging infectious diseases increasingly threaten wildlife populations. Most studies focus on managing short-term epidemic properties, such as controlling early outbreaks. Predicting long-term endemic characteristics with limited retrospective data is more challenging. We used individual-based modeling informed by individual variation in pathogen load and transmissibility to predict long-term impacts of a lethal, transmissible cancer on Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii) populations. For this, we employed approximate Bayesian computation to identify model scenarios that best matched known epidemiological and demographic system properties derived from 10 yr of data after disease emergence, enabling us to forecast future system dynamics. We show that the dramatic devil population declines observed thus far are likely attributable to transient dynamics (initial dynamics after disease emergence). Only 21% of matching scenarios led to devil extinction within 100 yr following devil facial tumor disease (DFTD) introduction, whereas DFTD faded out in 57% of simulations. In the remaining 22% of simulations, disease and host coexisted for at least 100 yr, usually with long-period oscillations. Our findings show that pathogen extirpation or host–pathogen coexistence are much more likely than the DFTD-induced devil extinction, with crucial management ramifications. Accounting for individual-level disease progression and the long-term outcome of devil–DFTD interactions at the population-level, our findings suggest that immediate management interventions are unlikely to be necessary to ensure the persistence of Tasmanian devil populations. This is because strong population declines of devils after disease emergence do not necessarily translate into long-term population declines at equilibria. Our modeling approach is widely applicable to other host–pathogen systems to predict disease impact beyond transient dynamics.

title: Host Specificity in Variable Environments

Review Article

Host Specificity in Variable Environments


Konstans Wells, Nicholas J. Clark


Full citation

Konstans Wells, Nicholas J. Clark (2019). Host Specificity in Variable Environments. Trends in Parasitology 35(6) 452-465 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pt.2019.04.001



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.








Research overview


The paper reframes host specificity from a static descriptive property to a dynamic eco-evolutionary process shaped jointly by evolutionary history, ecological opportunity and environmental filtering. By integrating niche theory, community ecology and epidemiological modelling, it establishes a theoretical foundation for distinguishing realized from fundamental host specificity and outlines how probabilistic, trait-based and network modelling approaches can improve forecasting of parasite spillover under environmental change.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Realized host specificity represents only the subset of host species that a parasite infects under particular environmental conditions and should not be interpreted as its complete fundamental host range.





Environmental filtering, host community composition and ecological opportunity interact with evolutionary history to generate spatial and temporal variation in realized host specificity.





Predicting parasite spillover and host shifting requires moving beyond static host-specificity indices towards modelling frameworks that explicitly account for environmental variation, uncertainty and ecological processes.





Trait-based models, ecological network approaches and probabilistic hierarchical models provide complementary tools for quantifying host specificity and identifying the ecological mechanisms underlying host–parasite interactions.





Forecasts of emerging infectious disease risk should distinguish between a parasite's realized host specificity observed under contemporary conditions and its potentially much broader fundamental capacity to infect novel host species.





Integrating ecological, evolutionary and environmental data within unified modelling frameworks provides a foundation for improving predictions of host shifting and emerging infectious diseases under global environmental change.






Key findings and propositions



Observed host ranges underestimate potential host breadth.


Environmental gradients alter realized host specificity.


Host phylogeny and functional similarity jointly influence host use.


Sampling bias substantially affects host specificity estimates.


Forecasting disease emergence requires integrating multiple data sources and uncertainty.

title: Climate variation influences host specificity in avian malaria parasites
text:
Research article

Climate variation influences host specificity in avian malaria parasites


Alan Fecchio, Konstans Wells, Jeffrey A. Bell, Vasyl V. Tkach, Holly L. Lutz, Jason D. Weckstein, Sonya M. Clegg, Nicholas J. Clark


Full citation

Fecchio, A., Wells, K., Bell, J. A., Tkach, V. V., Lutz, H. L., Weckstein, J. D., Clegg, S. M., & Clark, N. J. (2019). Climate variation influences host specificity in avian malaria parasites. Ecology Letters, 22(3), 547-557. https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.13215



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study establishes that realised host specificity is environmentally contingent rather than an invariant parasite property. Most avian malaria parasites infected phylogenetically clustered subsets of available hosts, but the strength of this specialisation varied geographically. Rainfall seasonality and minimum rainfall during the driest quarter were the dominant regional predictors, suggesting that climate-mediated variation in vector activity, host aggregation and encounter opportunity shapes parasite host ranges.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Realised host specificity in avian malaria parasites varies among biogeographical regions and is therefore not a fixed parasite trait.





Most Plasmodium and Haemoproteus lineages infected phylogenetically clustered subsets of the avian hosts available within regional host pools.





Rainfall seasonality explained the largest proportion of regional variation in realised host specificity, with stronger seasonality associated with greater parasite specialisation.





Avian malaria parasites were more specialised in regions with wetter dry seasons, indicating that precipitation during climatically limiting periods influences host-range structure.





Regional variation in host specificity was robust to differences in sampling effort, host diversity and parasite richness.





Parasite-level specialisation was driven more strongly by host phylogenetic relatedness than by ecological similarity in diet and foraging habitat.





Parasite communities in Brazilian Amazonia, Peru, Malaysia and Melanesia were among the least specialised, whereas those in New Zealand, the Philippines and south-eastern Australia were more specialised relative to local host pools.





Seasonal rainfall may concentrate vectors and breeding birds in time and space, increasing transmission among a narrower subset of hosts and selecting for greater host specialisation.





Hierarchical models that partition parasite- and region-level effects provide a framework for estimating geographically variable host specificity from observed host-association data.





Climate-dependent host specificity should be incorporated into predictions of parasite host shifting and infectious disease emergence under global climate change.

title: Disentangling synergistic disease dynamics: Implications for the viral biocontrol of rabbits
text:
Research article

Disentangling synergistic disease dynamics: Implications for the viral biocontrol of rabbits


Konstans Wells, Damien A. Fordham, Barry W. Brook, Phillip Cassey, Tarnya Cox, Robert B. O’Hara, Nina I. Schwensow


Full citation

Wells, K., Fordham, D. A., Brook, B. W., Cassey, P., Cox, T., O’Hara, R. B., & Schwensow, N. I. (2018). Disentangling synergistic disease dynamics: Implications for the viral biocontrol of rabbits. Journal of Animal Ecology, 87(5), 1418-1428. https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2656.12871



Publisher article

It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




State-space inference framework for estimating disease-specific survival and infection dynamics in European rabbits. Observed and unobserved capture histories are linked to age, maternal antibodies, susceptibility, immunity and death, allowing latent disease states and transitions to be estimated throughout each individual's life. Credit: Wells et al. (2018); illustration prepared by David Sargent




Research overview


The study demonstrates that rabbit viral biocontrol dynamics are shaped by persistent transmission, seasonal variation in force of infection and delayed effects of prior infection on survival. Rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus produced immediate survival costs, whereas myxoma virus appeared to reduce later survival among individuals that survived initial infection. Despite strong annual fluctuations, no long-term decline in infection rates or disease-induced mortality was detected.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus infection was strongly seasonal but susceptible rabbits were likely exposed throughout most of the year.





Rabbits susceptible to rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus had monthly survival probabilities approximately 25% lower than immune rabbits.





The average monthly force of rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus infection in winter and spring was approximately 38%, producing an estimated infection-induced mortality rate of about 69%.





Individuals susceptible to both rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus and myxoma virus had higher survival than rabbits susceptible to rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus but immune to myxoma virus.





The lower survival of rabbits that had survived myxoma virus infection suggests that myxomatosis can impose delayed demographic costs beyond the acute infection period.





Forces of infection for rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus and myxoma virus were strongly correlated, indicating synchrony in the epidemiological dynamics of the two diseases.





No long-term trend was detected in infection rates or disease-induced mortality for either rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus or myxoma virus during the 17-year study.





Continuous low-level transmission, heterogeneous transmission routes and variation in infectious dose may reduce the population-level efficacy of rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus as a biocontrol agent.





Bayesian multistate capture–mark–recapture models can jointly estimate latent disease states, survival, seroconversion and force of infection when infection histories are only partially observed.





Improving rabbit biocontrol requires attention to transmission timing, routes and infectious dose in addition to the virulence of released viral strains.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.



European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) have been exposed to rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus (RHDV) and myxoma virus (MYXV) in their native and invasive ranges for decades. Yet, the long-term effects of these viruses on rabbit population dynamics remain poorly understood. 2. In this context, we analysed 17 years of detailed capture–mark–recapture data (2000–2016) from Turretfield, South Australia, using a probabilistic state-space hierarchical modelling framework to estimate rabbit survival and epidemiological dynamics. 3. While RHDV infection and disease-induced death were most prominent during annual epidemics in winter and spring, we found evidence for continuous infection of susceptible individuals with RHDV throughout the year. RHDV-susceptible rabbits had, on average, 25% lower monthly survival rates compared to immune individuals, while the average monthly force of infection in winter and spring was ~38%. These combined to result in an average infection-induced mortality rate of 69% in winter and spring. 4. Individuals susceptible to MYXV and immune to RHDV had similar survival probabilities to those having survived infections from both viruses, whereas individuals susceptible to both RHDV and MYXV had higher survival probabilities than those susceptible to RHDV and immune to MYXV. This suggests that MYXV may reduce the future survival rates of individuals that endure initial MYXV infection. 5. There was no evidence for long-term changes in disease-induced mortality and infection rates for either RHDV or MYXV. 6. We conclude that continuous, year-round virus perpetuation (and perhaps heterogeneity in modes of transmission and infectious doses during and after epidemics) acts to reduce the efficiency of RHDV and MYXV as biocontrol agents of rabbits in their invasive range. However, if virulence can be maintained as relatively constant through time, RHDV and MYXV will likely continue realizing strong benefits as biocontrol agents.

Parasite spread at the domestic animal-wildlife interface: anthropogenic habitat use, phylogeny and body mass drive risk of cat and dog flea (Ctenocephalides spp.) infestation in wild mammals

Full citation

Parasite spread at the domestic animal-wildlife interface: anthropogenic habitat use, phylogeny and body mass drive risk of cat and dog flea (Ctenocephalides spp.) infestation in wild mammals. Research overview


The study provides one of the first global macroecological analyses of flea spillover between domestic animals and wildlife. By integrating systematic host–parasite records with phylogenetic comparative modelling and functional-phylogenetic host specificity analyses, it demonstrates that host evolutionary history and ecological traits jointly determine parasite infestation risk. The findings distinguish two contrasting spillover strategies: the broadly host-generalist cat flea, capable of ecological fitting across diverse mammalian lineages, and the more phylogenetically constrained dog flea. The work advances understanding of parasite host switching, invasive reservoir hosts and disease emergence at the human–domestic animal–wildlife interface within a One Health framework.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Cat fleas (Ctenocephalides felis) are extreme host generalists that infest a broad phylogenetic diversity of wild mammal species, whereas dog fleas (Ctenocephalides canis) are largely restricted to a limited number of closely related mammalian lineages.





Wildlife species that use anthropogenic habitats have substantially higher probabilities of cat flea infestation, indicating that human-modified environments facilitate parasite spillover at the domestic animal–wildlife interface.





Host phylogeny, body mass and anthropogenic habitat use jointly explain variation in flea infestation risk, demonstrating that both evolutionary history and ecological traits shape host susceptibility to parasite spillover.





Invasive and free-ranging mammals, including feral cats, feral dogs, red foxes, black rats and brown rats, function as important reservoir hosts that increase opportunities for flea transmission between domestic animals and wildlife.





Reducing contact between wildlife and domestic or invasive reservoir hosts across both natural and anthropogenic habitats is a key strategy for limiting flea spillover and the spread of flea-borne pathogens at the human–domestic animal–wildlife interface.

Interglacial refugia on tropical mountains: Novel insights from the summit rat (Rattus baluensis), a Borneo mountain endemic


Miguel Camacho-Sanchez, Irene Quintanilla, Melissa T. R. Hawkins, Fred Y. Y. Tuh, Konstans Wells, Jesus E. Maldonado, Jennifer A. Leonard


Full citation

Camacho-Sanchez, M., Quintanilla, I., Hawkins, M. T. R., Tuh, F. Y. Y., Wells, K., Maldonado, J. E., & Leonard, J. A. (2018). Interglacial refugia on tropical mountains: Novel insights from the summit rat (Rattus baluensis), a Borneo mountain endemic. Distribution, habitat association and genetic structure of the summit rat across Mount Kinabalu and Mount Tambuyukon. The species was recorded mainly in upper montane forest and scrubland above 2,000 m, including sites with Nepenthes rajah. Genetic ancestry estimates identify two distinct populations corresponding to the two mountains, despite their separation by less than 18 km. Credit: Camacho-Sanchez et al. (2018); summit rat photograph by Ch’ien C. Lee




Research overview


The study provides empirical evidence that tropical mountain endemics can persist in interglacial refugia formed by post-glacial upslope habitat contraction. Summit rats on Mount Kinabalu and Mount Tambuyukon are genetically isolated, with the smaller Tambuyukon population retaining less genetic diversity. Their inferred Holocene split accords with the retreat of upper-montane forest after the Last Glacial Maximum and illustrates how elevational habitat barriers can generate strong population structure over short geographical distances.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






The summit rat occurs in upper montane mossy forest, dwarf forest and scrubland above approximately 2,000 m on Mount Kinabalu and Mount Tambuyukon in Sabah, Borneo.





Discovery of a second summit rat population on Mount Tambuyukon expanded the known distribution of a species previously considered endemic to Mount Kinabalu.





Nuclear and mitochondrial genetic data identify the Mount Kinabalu and Mount Tambuyukon summit rats as strongly differentiated and effectively isolated populations.





Approximately 22% of nuclear and mitochondrial genetic variation was partitioned between the two mountains, despite their separation by less than 18 km.





Genetic diversity and estimated effective population size were higher on Mount Kinabalu than on Mount Tambuyukon.





Approximate Bayesian computation supports fragmentation of a larger ancestral summit rat population during the Holocene, with population separation estimated at approximately 3,000 years ago.





The lower-elevation forest between Mount Kinabalu and Mount Tambuyukon functions as a dispersal barrier for a species specialised on cool upper-montane habitat.





The summit rat's current genetic structure is consistent with interglacial refugia formed when upland forest retreated to higher elevations after the Last Glacial Maximum.





Continued climatic warming is expected to contract suitable summit rat habitat upslope, placing the lower Mount Tambuyukon population at particularly high extinction risk.





High tropical mountains can preserve endemic biodiversity during climatic warming by retaining cool habitat above the elevational limits available on lower peaks.





Multi-locus nuclear markers, complete mitochondrial genomes and approximate Bayesian computation provide complementary evidence for recent fragmentation and demographic history in isolated mountain populations.

Conceptual framework for targeting invasive European rabbit control by season and age class. Control actions differ in their capacity to affect juveniles, subadults and adults, and in operational constraints, efficacy, frequency and seasonal timing. Credit: Konstans Wells et al. (2016), The Wildlife Society




Research overview


The study inferred age-structured seasonal survival from long-term rabbit monitoring and propagated those estimates into stochastic population simulations. It showed that juvenile-only control has little demographic effect, whereas interventions affecting subadults, adults or all age classes can substantially suppress populations. Control efficacy dominates the speed of extirpation, but targeting age classes with high reproductive value is essential for achieving extirpation at all. The work demonstrates how demographic evidence can be used to design seasonally targeted invasive species management.

Control measures targeting only juvenile European rabbits have negligible effects on long-term population size because juveniles contribute less reproductive value than older age classes.





Control actions that affect subadult and adult rabbits produce larger population reductions, particularly when applied after the breeding season.





Significant rabbit population reductions and local extirpation require control actions that affect all age groups and achieve high efficacy.





Even annual control causing 95% mortality does not guarantee rapid local extirpation; successful simulations required an average of 119 weeks in the absence of immigration.





Age class has the strongest influence on whether simulated rabbit populations are extirpated, whereas control efficacy has the strongest influence on time to extirpation.





Effective invasive-rabbit management should explicitly account for seasonal demography and target individuals with high reproductive potential rather than focusing only on abundant juvenile cohorts.





The balance between control intensity and intervention frequency governs local population suppression, extirpation and recovery in species with recurrent population oscillations.

Effects of metapopulation topology and spatial management strategy on invasive-species control. The upper row shows star, ring, neighbour, ring-random, ring-hub and scale-free networks. Lower panels compare general population reduction with reduction of an obligate resource as management extent increases. Resource reduction generally produces larger declines, while targeting highly connected populations is most beneficial in heterogeneous networks. Credit: Lurgi et al. (2016)




Research overview


The study demonstrates that invasive-species management outcomes emerge from interactions among network topology, dispersal and intervention design. Resource reduction consistently outperformed direct removal, especially when applied broadly. Targeting central populations added value in heterogeneous networks, but had little effect in homogeneous, highly connected rabbit landscapes where recolonisation pathways were widely distributed.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Reduction of an obligate resource was generally more effective than direct population removal for lowering invasive-species abundance at landscape scales.





Management extent was the dominant determinant of control success across most simulated invasive-species metapopulations.





Spatially targeting highly connected or neighbouring populations improved control most strongly in metapopulation networks with heterogeneous link distributions.





In homogeneous and highly connected metapopulations, random, clustered and hub-targeted spatial management strategies produced similar outcomes.





In model star and scale-free networks, management targeted at central populations reduced metapopulation abundance more effectively than random management.





Reducing carrying capacity by 60% in 90% of local populations decreased simulated metapopulation abundance by up to 50% at intermediate dispersal.





Direct population reduction produced substantial declines only when a large proportion of local populations was managed or dispersal was very low or very high.





For real-world rabbit landscapes in Western Australia, management extent and intensity were more important than the spatial rule used to select local populations.





Landscape connectivity mediates the value of spatial prioritisation because immigration from connected source populations can rapidly restore locally depleted populations.





Simulation frameworks that integrate demography, dispersal, network topology and management capacity can identify efficient landscape-scale invasive-species control strategies.





Detailed spatial planning should be prioritised for small or heterogeneously connected invasive-species networks, whereas highly homogeneous networks require broad management coverage rather than complex targeting.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Biological invasions are not only a major threat to biodiversity, they also have major impacts on local economies and agricultural production systems. Once established, the connection of local populations into metapopulation networks facilitates dispersal at landscape scales, generating spatial dynamics that can impact the outcome of pest-management actions. Much planning goes into landscape-scale invasive species management. However, effective management requires knowledge on the interplay between metapopulation network topology and management actions. We address this knowledge gap using simulation models to explore the effectiveness of two common management strategies, applied across different extents and according to different rules for selecting target localities in metapopulations with different network topologies. These management actions are: (i) general population reduction, and (ii) reduction of an obligate resource. The reduction of an obligate resource was generally more efficient than population reduction for depleting populations at landscape scales. However, the way in which local populations are selected for management is important when the topology of the metapopulation is heterogeneous in terms of the distribution of connections among local populations. We tested these broad findings using real-world scenarios of European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) infesting agricultural landscapes in Western Australia. Although management strategies targeting central populations were more effective in simulated heterogeneous metapopulation structures, no difference was observed in real-world metapopulation structures that are highly homogeneous. In large metapopulations with high proximity and connectivity of neighbouring populations, different spatial management strategies yield similar outcomes. Directly considering spatial attributes in pest-management actions will be most important for metapopulation networks with heterogeneously distributed links. Our modelling framework provides a simple approach for identifying the best possible management strategy for invasive species based on metapopulation structure and control capacity. This information can be used by managers trying to devise efficient landscape-oriented management strategies for invasive species and can also generate insights for conservation purposes.

Research overview


The study links parasite occurrence in invasive rats to both regional parasite geography and the composition of local mammal host assemblages. Parasite richness and turnover varied strongly among zoogeographic regions, while infection probabilities in rats closely tracked the prevalence of the same parasites in local wildlife hosts. The modelling framework also addressed incomplete sampling and false absences, allowing species-level and community-level information to be combined.

A global database contained 241 helminth parasite species associated with the Rattus rattus species complex and Rattus norvegicus, including 65 parasite species recorded from both invasive hosts.





Helminth parasite richness and assemblage turnover showed strong biogeographic structure, with the lowest estimated richness and most distinctive assemblages in Madagascar and the highest richness in the Palaearctic or Oriental regions, depending on host species.





Parasite species richness and regional turnover were correlated between Rattus rattus and Rattus norvegicus, although their parasite assemblages within the same regions were often distinct.





Infection probability of invasive rats with a parasite was strongly related to the estimated infection probability of the local mammal host assemblage with that parasite.





Local wildlife-host infection probability significantly influenced infection estimates for 114 of 241 parasite species in Rattus rattus and 128 parasite species in Rattus norvegicus.





Parasite occurrence in other mammal hosts decreased with increasing taxonomic distance from the genus Rattus and with increasing conservation threat status.





Climate-zone occurrence explained infection probability for relatively few parasite species compared with the effects of local wildlife-host assemblages.





Forecasting disease emergence in invasive hosts requires models that integrate parasite biogeography, local host-community composition and incomplete observation of host–parasite associations.

Full citation

Research overview


The model decomposed observed abundance into persistence at the same site, movement among neighbouring sites and migration to or from a wider regional pool. Species differed markedly in mobility and site fidelity, but the strongest temporal structure was consistently monthly rather than annual. Winter temperature influenced abundance across species, demonstrating that short-term weather and movement processes can dominate local count dynamics.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






A spatially explicit hidden Markov model separated site persistence, movement among neighbouring water bodies and migration to or from a regional population pool using counts of unmarked waterbirds.





Across seven waterbird species monitored at 122 sites, abundance in the preceding month explained approximately 12%–47% of variation in regional abundance fluctuations.





Variation in site-specific density effects was substantially greater among months than among years for all seven species.





Movements among adjacent surveyed sites explained little modelled variation, whereas site persistence and migration to or from the wider population pool differed strongly among species.





Common teal and common pochard showed the strongest site fidelity after arrival but also the strongest regional migration.





Mallard, tufted duck and great crested grebe behaved more like integrated regional populations because individuals moved more frequently among sites and local abundance was less dependent on regional migration alone.





Abundance increased with warmer January or February temperatures for all species, while the strength of temperature effects varied mainly among months rather than among years.





Population monitoring of mobile species should represent movement and environmental drivers at monthly or similarly fine temporal scales rather than relying only on annual trends.

Conceptual framework linking per-individual interactions to species-level ecological networks. Individual resource and consumer observations retain information about sampling effort, species abundance, interaction rates and zero encounters, whereas aggregation into a species-level network can make differently sampled species appear to have similar interaction strength. Credit: Wells and O’Hara (2013)




Research overview


The paper formalises ecological network formation as a hierarchy linking individual behaviour, species abundance and community-level network structure. It shows that aggregated interaction frequencies confound biological interaction strength with sample size and population pools, whereas individual-level models preserve zero encounters, estimate uncertainty and accommodate environmental covariates and detection effects.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Species-level interaction frequencies in ecological networks combine per-individual interaction strength with the numbers of sampled or available individuals and therefore cannot be interpreted independently of abundance and sampling effort.





Aggregating individual observations into species-level adjacency matrices discards information about non-interacting individuals, observation effort and environmental conditions.





Small sample sizes caused the network-level specialization index H2 to be overestimated when calculated directly from aggregated interaction data.





With equal sampling, aggregated estimates of network specialization approached the exhaustive-sampling value only when approximately 15 or more individuals per species were sampled.





Unequal sample sizes among species produced increasingly biased estimates of network specialization from aggregated data even when total sample size increased.





Individual-level hierarchical models estimated per-species interaction strengths close to their generating values even under small sample sizes, while explicitly representing uncertainty.





Individual-level models distinguished true absence of interaction from false zero observations through a species-pair interaction indicator.





Estimates of network specialization derived from the individual-level model were robust to heterogeneous sample sizes and improved as sample size increased.





Per-individual interaction strength should be separated from per-species interaction frequency because the latter is inevitably influenced by species abundance.





Hierarchical interaction models can incorporate individual traits, species attributes, environmental covariates, detection error and temporal or spatial variation before network metrics are calculated.





Ecological network databases should retain individual-level observations and detailed sampling protocols rather than storing only aggregated interaction matrices.





Comparative network studies risk ecological fallacies when differences created by sampling design are interpreted as biological differences among species or communities.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.



Ecological network models based on aggregated data from species interactions are widely used to make inferences about species specialization, functionality and extinction risk. While increasing number of network data are available and are used in comparative studies, data quality and uncertainty have received little attention. Moreover, key individual-level information such as the proportion of individuals not involved in interactions and underlying processes driving interactions are ignored by aggregated data analysis. 2. We suggest an individual-level hierarchical interaction model as a more flexible approach to considering uncertainty, sampling effort and conditions under which interactions take place and from which network attributes can be derived. We performed a simulation exercise to compare inference under different sample sizes and from aggregated data matrices to those from our individual-level model. 3. Formalizing the process of network formation in an individual-level model made clear that per-species interaction frequencies are not independent of sample size and population pools and also ignore important information given by the proportion of non-interacting individuals. Hierarchical linear models are a possible solution to infer community-level attributes of network formation and allow various kinds of comprehensive model extensions to capture variation of per-individual interactions in space and time that shape upper level organization. 4. Individual-level hierarchical models provide the link between individual behaviour and interactions under variable environmental conditions and can be summarized into networks in a conceptually neat way. Such models may not only help to account for various sources of variation but also conceptualize aspects overlooked in aggregated data. In particular, the quantification of per-individual interactions under different sampling scenarios emphasizes that per-species interaction frequencies at the species level are not necessarily a surrogate of species abundance in natural systems under investigation.

Variable strength of forest stand attributes and weather conditions on the questing activity of Ixodes ricinus ticks over years in managed forests


Ralf Lauterbach, Konstans Wells, Robert B. O’Hara, Elisabeth K. V. Kalko, Swen C. Renner


Full citation

Research overview


The publication links forest management, climate variability and vector ecology by showing that young successional stands supported higher questing nymph densities, while preceding winter temperature strongly influenced abundance across years. Single-year effects differed from pooled multi-year patterns, demonstrating that habitat and weather drivers operate differently across spatial and temporal scales.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Questing Ixodes ricinus nymphs were more abundant in young thicket-stage forest stands than in pole-wood and timber-stage stands in managed forests of south-west Germany.





Forest successional stage explained approximately 17% of variation in relative questing nymph abundance across the three study years.





Increasing herb-layer cover was associated with lower sampled nymph density and explained approximately 25% of variation in the full model.





Across 2008–2010, a one-degree Celsius increase in mean winter temperature was associated with an estimated 82% increase in relative questing nymph density.





The direction and magnitude of weather effects differed among years; in 2008, warmer sites had fewer questing nymphs even though milder winters were associated with higher density across years.





Spring precipitation was the strongest measured predictor in 2010, when wetter conditions were associated with increased nymph density.





Forest management can influence tick questing activity through stand age and vegetation structure, but interannual weather may override or reverse habitat effects.





Robust assessment of tick abundance and disease risk requires multi-year monitoring that jointly measures forest structure, weather, microclimate and vertebrate host abundance.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Given the ever-increasing human impact through land use and climate change on the environment, we crucially need to achieve a better understanding of those factors that influence the questing activity of ixodid ticks, a major disease-transmitting vector in temperate forests. We investigated variation in the relative questing nymph densities of Ixodes ricinus in differently managed forest types for three years (2008–2010) in SW Germany by drag sampling. We used a hierarchical Bayesian modeling approach to examine the relative effects of habitat and weather and to consider possible nested structures of habitat and climate forces. The questing activity of nymphs was considerably larger in young forest successional stages of thicket compared with pole wood and timber stages. Questing nymph density increased markedly with milder winter temperatures. Generally, the relative strength of the various environmental forces on questing nymph density differed across years. In particular, winter temperature had a negative effect on tick activity across sites in 2008 in contrast to the overall effect of temperature across years. Our results suggest that forest management practices have important impacts on questing nymph density. Variable weather conditions, however, might override the effects of forest management practices on the fluctuations and dynamics of tick populations and activity over years, in particular, the preceding winter temperatures. Therefore, robust predictions and the detection of possible interactions and nested structures of habitat and climate forces can only be quantified through the collection of long-term data. Such data are particularly important with regard to future scenarios of forest management and climate warming.

Research overview


The study shows that different ectoparasite groups respond to distinct ecological scales. Flea and louse burdens were associated mainly with housing conditions, whereas tick density depended more strongly on dog habitat use and exposure to plantations and forests. Spatial clustering and elevational effects further shaped infestation probability, while the presence of wildlife-associated Haemaphysalis ticks highlighted possible transmission links across domestic-animal and wildlife systems.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Fleas infested 92% of sampled domestic dogs in Sabah, making them the most prevalent ectoparasite group in the study.





Ctenocephalides orientis and Ctenocephalides felis felis were the two flea species identified from domestic dogs, and both species frequently co-occurred on the same hosts.





Flea density was higher on dogs living in bamboo or corrugated-metal housing and lower on dogs associated with stone or compound housing.





Smaller dogs carried higher flea densities, whereas forest cover, human population density and other landscape-scale variables had weak explanatory power.





The invasive chewing louse Heterodoxus spiniger infested 20% of sampled dogs and was recorded only from dogs associated with stone or timber houses.





Tick infestation occurred on 17% of sampled dogs and included Rhipicephalus sanguineus and four Haemaphysalis taxa.





Dogs using both plantations and forests had an estimated 282% increase in overall tick density relative to the average dog.





Louse and tick infestation probabilities declined with elevation, with most infestations recorded below approximately 800 m above sea level.





Spatial autocorrelation explained substantial variation in the probability of louse and tick infestation but little variation in ectoparasite density among infested dogs.





Household-scale environmental conditions were more influential for flea and louse density than broad landscape-scale variables.





Overlap between dog-associated Haemaphysalis ticks and ticks recorded from forest wildlife identifies domestic dogs as potential bridge hosts for tick-borne pathogen transmission.





Studies of companion-animal ectoparasites in rapidly changing tropical landscapes should integrate host behaviour, housing, wildlife contact and land-use change.

Bartonella and Rickettsia in arthropods from the Lao PDR and from Borneo, Malaysia


Tahar Kernif, Cristina Socolovschi, Konstans Wells, Maklarin B. Lakim, Saythong Inthalad, Günther Slesak, Najma Boudebouch, Jean-Claude Beaucournu, Paul N. Newton, Didier Raoult, Philippe Parola


Full citation

Kernif, T., Socolovschi, C., Wells, K., Lakim, M. B., Inthalad, S., Slesak, G., Boudebouch, N., Beaucournu, J.-C., Newton, P. N., Raoult, D., & Parola, P. (2012). Bartonella and Rickettsia in arthropods from the Lao PDR and from Borneo, Malaysia. Comparative Immunology, Microbiology and Infectious Diseases, 35(1), 51–57. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cimid.2011.10.003

About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study expands understanding of arthropod-borne bacterial pathogens in Southeast Asia by demonstrating that domestic animal ectoparasites harbour multiple zoonotic bacteria with distinct prevalence patterns. It identifies both Ctenocephalides felis felis and Ctenocephalides orientis as carriers of Rickettsia felis, documents occasional co-infection with Bartonella clarridgeiae, and reports molecular evidence consistent with a previously undescribed Rickettsia lineage in Boophilus ticks. The findings highlight the value of molecular surveillance of ectoparasites for detecting recognised and emerging vector-borne pathogens.

Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Rickettsia felis is highly prevalent in Ctenocephalides fleas parasitising domestic dogs in both the Lao PDR and Malaysian Borneo, indicating widespread circulation of this zoonotic pathogen across geographically distinct regions of Southeast Asia.





Both Ctenocephalides felis felis and Ctenocephalides orientis function as natural carriers of Rickettsia felis within domestic dog flea communities in Southeast Asia.





Bartonella clarridgeiae occurs at low prevalence in flea populations from both study regions and can co-occur with Rickettsia felis within individual flea vectors.





Molecular characterization of Boophilus ticks collected from cattle in Laos identified a Rickettsia lineage with insufficient similarity to recognised species, suggesting the presence of a previously undescribed taxon.





Molecular surveillance of ectoparasites from domestic animals provides an effective approach for detecting both established and previously unrecognised zoonotic bacterial pathogens circulating within regional transmission systems.





Isolation and comprehensive characterization of the putative novel Rickettsia are required before its taxonomic status and epidemiological significance can be established.





The occurrence of Rickettsia felis and Bartonella clarridgeiae in common ectoparasites of domestic animals supports their continued investigation as potential contributors to undiagnosed febrile illness in Southeast Asia.

title: Pitchers of Nepenthes rajah collect faecal droppings from both diurnal and nocturnal small mammals and emit fruity odour
text:
Research article

Pitchers of Nepenthes rajah collect faecal droppings from both diurnal and nocturnal small mammals and emit fruity odour


Konstans Wells, Maklarin B. Lakim, Stefan Schulz, Manfred Ayasse


Full citation

Wells, K., Lakim, M. B., Schulz, S., & Ayasse, M. (2011). Pitchers of Nepenthes rajah collect faecal droppings from both diurnal and nocturnal small mammals and emit fruity odour. Journal of Tropical Ecology, 27(4), 347-353. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0266467411000162



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Small-mammal interactions with Nepenthes rajah at Mesilau, Borneo. The diurnal mountain tree shrew Tupaia montana and nocturnal summit rat Rattus baluensis repeatedly visited pitchers, balanced on the peristome and licked exudates from glands beneath the lid. Their posture facilitates deposition of faeces into the pitcher, creating a resource exchange between mammals and the carnivorous plant. Credit: Wells et al. (2011)




Research overview


The study expands the known vertebrate community associated with Nepenthes rajah by showing that both diurnal tree shrews and nocturnal rats repeatedly visit pitchers. Mammals obtain exudates from lid glands while depositing faeces into the pitcher, supporting a multi-species mutualistic interaction. The pitcher lids emit a complex bouquet of fruit- and flower-associated volatile compounds that may exploit shared sensory preferences across mammalian taxa.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Nepenthes rajah pitchers were visited frequently by both the diurnal mountain tree shrew Tupaia montana and the nocturnal summit rat Rattus baluensis.





Across 413.5 hours of camera and video observation, 56 visits by Tupaia montana and 42 visits by Rattus baluensis were recorded, equivalent to one small-mammal visit every 4.2 hours on average.





Both mammal species typically stood on the pitcher rim and licked exudates from glands on the inner surface of the pitcher lid.





The feeding posture of visiting mammals positioned their hindquarters above the pitcher opening, allowing faecal pellets to fall directly into the pitcher.





Fresh faecal droppings from small mammals accumulated in surveyed pitchers at an average rate of one deposition event every 3.4 days.





Only one drowned Tupaia montana was found among 42 repeatedly surveyed mature pitchers, indicating that vertebrate capture was rare relative to repeated faecal deposition.





Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry identified 44 volatile compounds emitted from Nepenthes rajah pitcher lids, including hydrocarbons, alcohols, esters, ketones and six sulphur-containing compounds.





Many volatiles emitted by Nepenthes rajah are also present in fruits and flowers, supporting the hypothesis that pitcher odour contributes to attracting small mammals.





The interaction between Nepenthes rajah and small mammals is consistent with a mutualistic resource exchange in which mammals receive sugary exudates and the plant receives nutrient-rich faeces.





Nepenthes rajah is not specialised exclusively for tree shrews because both diurnal tree shrews and nocturnal rats repeatedly use the pitchers.





Faecal inputs may alter the pitcher microenvironment and create secondary trophic effects by attracting flies and midges that can themselves enter the pitcher.





Future experiments should separate the relative contributions of visual signals, olfactory cues and specific volatile compounds to mammal attraction.

title: Host specificity and niche partitioning in flea–small mammal networks in Bornean rainforests
text:
Research article

Host specificity and niche partitioning in flea–small mammal networks in Bornean rainforests


Konstans Wells, Maklarin B. Lakim, Jean-Claude Beaucournu


Full citation

Wells, K., Lakim, M. B., & Beaucournu, J.-C. (2011). Host specificity and niche partitioning in flea–small mammal networks in Bornean rainforests. Medical and Veterinary Entomology, 25(3), 311-319. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2915.2010.00940.x



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study provides one of the first community-level analyses of tropical flea–mammal networks in Southeast Asia. It shows intermediate but non-random complementary specialization, broad flea sharing among treeshrews and squirrels, and a distinctive rat-associated network dominated by Sigmactenus alticola. Host specificity also varied between lowland and montane forests, linking network structure to environmental and functional differences among host groups.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






The montane field survey recorded 234 individual fleas representing eight flea species on seven non-volant small mammal species.





Fleas were detected on 74 of 90 sampled small mammals, corresponding to an overall infestation prevalence of approximately 82%.





Up to three flea species co-occurred on individual treeshrews and squirrels, with a mean of 1.3 flea species per infested host.





The field-survey network showed intermediate complementary specialization and differed significantly from random flea–host association.





The three most commonly recorded flea species, Gryphopsylla mjoebergi, Macrostylophora traubi and Lentistivalius vomerus, exhibited low host specificity across treeshrews and squirrels.





The compiled Bornean network contained 45 recorded associations among 15 flea species and 16 small mammal species.





Tupaia montana had the largest known flea assemblage in the compiled network, with nine flea species recorded.





Host specificity was higher among lowland flea–host associations than among montane associations.





Sigmactenus alticola was recorded on five of six rat species and on Tupaia montana, indicating broad host use across lowland and montane habitats.





Flea–host network structure differed among functional host groups, with diurnal treeshrews and squirrels sharing several flea species while nocturnal rats were dominated by one common flea taxon.





Complementary specialization indices provided broadly consistent community-level patterns between the short-term field survey and the literature-derived network despite incomplete sampling.





Incomplete sampling particularly biases inference for rarely encountered species, singleton interactions, network connectivity and modularity.





Differences in flea host specificity between lowland and montane forests may reflect climatic constraints, host nesting ecology and the availability of suitable microhabitats for flea development.





Changes in forest use and wildlife–commensal rodent contact may alter vector-borne disease transmission through shifts in flea abundance, host sharing and habitat tolerance.





Future research should combine repeated field sampling, environmental covariates and both host and parasite perspectives to explain variation in flea–host interaction intensity.

title: Seed consumption by small mammals from Borneo
text:
Research article

Seed consumption by small mammals from Borneo


Konstans Wells, Richard T. Corlett, Maklarin B. Lakim, Elisabeth K. V. Kalko, Martin Pfeiffer


Full citation

Wells, K., Corlett, R. T., Lakim, M. B., Kalko, E. K. V., & Pfeiffer, M. (2009). Seed consumption by small mammals from Borneo. Journal of Tropical Ecology, 25(5), 555-558. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0266467409990058



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Small mammals as seed consumers and potential seed dispersers in Bornean rain forests. The Bornean spiny rat (Maxomys rajah) is shown alongside examples of seeds recovered from faecal samples. Numerous intact fig (Ficus) seeds demonstrate that very small seeds can survive passage through the digestive tract and may subsequently be dispersed, whereas fragments of larger unidentified seeds illustrate seed predation. The study revealed that seed consumption is widespread among tropical rats and tree shrews, highlighting their diverse roles in seed dispersal and seed predation within forest regeneration processes. Credit: Konstans Wells




Research overview


The study provides evidence that diverse Bornean small mammals consume and potentially disperse seeds. Rodents had a higher incidence of seeds in faeces than tree shrews, figs were the most frequent identifiable seed resource, and seed integrity varied among host species. Higher seed occurrence in two rat species from logged forests suggests that land-use change can alter mammal–plant interaction strength.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Seeds were detected in 138 of 701 faecal samples collected from 13 non-volant small-mammal species in Bornean forests.





At least 11 seed morphotypes were distinguished from the faecal samples using seed size, shape, colour and surface characteristics.





Rat faecal samples contained seeds significantly more often than tree-shrew samples, with seeds present in 23% of rat samples and 13% of tree-shrew samples.





Leopoldamys sabanus had the highest observed proportion of faecal samples containing seeds among commonly sampled species, with seeds recorded in 48 of 145 samples.





Maxomys whiteheadi had significantly fewer seed-containing samples than Leopoldamys sabanus.





Fig seeds occurred in 74 of 701 samples and were recorded from nearly all commonly captured small-mammal species.





A larger seed morphotype measuring approximately 2.5–6 millimetres was found intact in faeces of Leopoldamys sabanus, Tupaia longipes and Tupaia tana but commonly fragmented in samples from smaller Maxomys species and Niviventer cremoriventer.





The largest swallowed seed recorded in the study measured 5.8 millimetres and occurred in a sample from Tupaia longipes.





Seed occurrence in faeces of Leopoldamys sabanus and Maxomys rajah was significantly higher in logged forests than in unlogged forests.





No clear difference in the identity of seed morphotypes was detected between logged and unlogged forests.





Rats may contribute more substantially to tropical forest seed dispersal than previously assumed because they are abundant, species rich and active across multiple forest strata.





Seed fate after ingestion is likely to vary among small-mammal species because body size, jaw strength, feeding behaviour and digestive physiology affect whether seeds remain intact.





Tree shrews may disperse seeds over relatively short distances because their simple digestive tract produces rapid food passage.





Forest logging can alter seed-consumption patterns indirectly by changing both small-mammal assemblages and the availability of fruit resources.





Faecal seed screening can reveal broad patterns of frugivory and seed consumption but cannot determine dispersal effectiveness without seed identification and viability testing.





Future research should quantify species-specific interaction strength, seed viability and dispersal distance across different forest types.

title: Diverse MHC IIB allele repertoire increases parasite resistance and body condition in the Long-tailed giant rat (Leopoldamys sabanus)
text:
Research article

Diverse MHC IIB allele repertoire increases parasite resistance and body condition in the Long-tailed giant rat (Leopoldamys sabanus)


Tobias L. Lenz, Konstans Wells, Martin Pfeiffer, Simone Sommer


Full citation

Lenz, T. L., Wells, K., Pfeiffer, M., & Sommer, S. (2009). Diverse MHC IIB allele repertoire increases parasite resistance and body condition in the Long-tailed giant rat (Leopoldamys sabanus). BMC Evolutionary Biology, 9, 269. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2148-9-269



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The publication links immune-gene variation to parasite resistance and host condition under natural tropical conditions. Highly polymorphic MHC class IIB alleles showed signatures of balancing selection, while individuals with more divergent allele combinations had fewer helminth morphotypes and better body condition. The findings provide field evidence for heterozygote and divergent-allele advantage.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Forty-six wild Leopoldamys sabanus individuals carried 28 distinct MHC class IIB nucleotide alleles, corresponding to 26 distinct amino-acid variants.





MHC class IIB exon 2 showed strong signatures of balancing and positive selection, especially at antigen-binding sites.





Individual rats carried between one and four MHC class IIB alleles, and allele number was positively correlated with within-individual allele divergence.





Greater within-individual MHC allele divergence was associated with improved body condition.





Greater within-individual MHC allele divergence was associated with lower helminth parasite species richness.





Individuals carrying more than one MHC class IIB allele had better body condition and lower parasite species richness than individuals with only one detected allele.





The results support both heterozygote advantage and the more specific divergent-allele-advantage hypothesis as mechanisms maintaining MHC polymorphism in a wild tropical mammal.





Associations between MHC diversity, parasite resistance and body condition demonstrate how host–parasite interactions can maintain immune genetic diversity under natural rainforest conditions.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Background: Genes of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) code for key functions in the adaptive immune response of vertebrates and most of them show exceptionally high polymorphism. This polymorphism has been associated with selection by diverse and changing parasite communities. We analysed MHC class IIB diversity, gastrointestinal parasite load and body condition in the wild-ranging tropical rat Leopoldamys sabanus under natural selection conditions in a highly variable rainforest environment in Borneo to explore the mechanisms that maintain these high levels of genetic polymorphism. Results: Allelic diversity was determined via SSCP and sequencing, and parasite screening was done through non-invasive faecal egg counts. The detected alleles showed high levels of polymorphism and signatures of balancing selection. More diverse MHC genotypes were associated with better body condition and resistance against helminth infection, and the data also suggested a positive effect of MHC allele divergence within individuals on these parameters. Conclusion: In accordance with the heterozygote-advantage hypothesis, this study provides evidence for an advantage of more diverse MHC genotypes. More specifically, the negative relationship between individual allele divergence and number of parasite species is consistent with the divergent-allele-advantage hypothesis.
