title: Movement and ranging patterns of a tropical rat (Leopoldamys sabanus) in logged and unlogged rain forests
text:
Research article

Movement and ranging patterns of a tropical rat (Leopoldamys sabanus) in logged and unlogged rain forests


Konstans Wells, Elisabeth K. V. Kalko, Maklarin B. Lakim, Martin Pfeiffer


Full citation

Wells, K., Kalko, E. K. V., Lakim, M. B., & Pfeiffer, M. (2008). Movement and ranging patterns of a tropical rat (Leopoldamys sabanus) in logged and unlogged rain forests. Journal of Mammalogy, 89(3), 712-720. https://doi.org/10.1644/07-MAMM-A-074R2.1



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Long-tailed giant rat (Leopoldamys sabanus) photographed while climbing in Bornean rainforest. This common forest rodent was the focal species for quantifying fine-scale movement paths and home-ranging behaviour in logged and unlogged tropical forests, providing insights into how forest disturbance influences animal movement and habitat connectivity. Photograph © Konstans Wells. Credit: Konstans Wells




Research overview


The study found no strong effect of logging on movement geometry, activity, speed or home-range size. Instead, substantial differences among individuals dominated the data. Movement paths combined clusters of short, slow moves with occasional long movements, consistent with searching in a patchy rainforest resource landscape.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Fine-scale movements of Leopoldamys sabanus were quantified from 49 spool-and-line tracks, while larger-scale ranging was measured by radiotracking 16 individuals for at least four consecutive nights.





Step-length distributions followed a power-law pattern and did not differ significantly between logged and unlogged forests.





Mean turning angles and the frequency of persistent, relatively straight fine-scale paths did not differ between forest types.





Approximately two thirds of spool-and-line tracks showed directional persistence rather than random turning.





Radiotracked rats were active for an average of approximately 485 minutes per night and travelled about 1,443 metres per night.





Nightly activity duration, total distance travelled and movement speed did not differ significantly between logged and unlogged forests or between sexes.





Movement-speed distributions resembled Lévy-walk patterns, with many short movements interspersed with occasional long movements.





Consecutive movement speeds were serially correlated, indicating that rats often made clusters of short, slow movements within local areas.





Nocturnal home ranges varied from approximately 2,083 to 9,829 square metres, while core ranges varied from 594 to 1,535 square metres.





Home-range and core-range sizes did not differ significantly between logged and unlogged forests or between sexes.





Individual variation in movement speed, activity duration, nightly path length and range size was substantially greater than variation explained by forest type or sex.





Local habitat structure and patchy resource distributions are more plausible drivers of movement variation than the broad classification of forest as logged or unlogged.





Logging-related changes in vegetation structure do not necessarily translate into detectable movement or ranging changes for a common habitat-generalist rat.





Plasticity in movement and search behaviour may allow common small mammals to persist in logged forests when sufficient environmental heterogeneity and resources remain.





Movement responses to habitat modification should be studied at multiple spatial scales because fine-scale trajectories and larger-scale ranging may respond to different ecological drivers.





Conservation assessments should avoid assuming that broad structural differences between logged and unlogged forests predict movement responses for all small-mammal species.

title: Impact of rain-forest logging on helminth assemblages in small mammals (Muridae, Tupaiidae) from Borneo
text:
Research article

Impact of rain-forest logging on helminth assemblages in small mammals (Muridae, Tupaiidae) from Borneo


Konstans Wells, Lesley R. Smales, Elisabeth K. V. Kalko, Martin Pfeiffer


Full citation

Wells, K., Smales, L. R., Kalko, E. K. V., & Pfeiffer, M. (2007). Impact of rain-forest logging on helminth assemblages in small mammals (Muridae, Tupaiidae) from Borneo. Journal of Tropical Ecology, 23, 35-43. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0266467406003804



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study demonstrates that anthropogenic forest disturbance can restructure host-parasite interactions through changes in habitat, microclimate, host performance, diet and transmission opportunities. Its central contribution is evidence that parasite responses to logging cannot be inferred from habitat disturbance alone because different host-parasite systems respond in contrasting ways.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Rain-forest logging altered the composition and abundance of helminth assemblages in Bornean small mammals, but the direction and magnitude of change differed among host species.





Nematode eggs occurred in 95% of the 337 faecal samples, with Strongylida most prevalent in Leopoldamys sabanus, Tupaia tana and Tupaia longipes, while Spirurida dominated in Niviventer cremoriventer.





Tupaia longipes had greater nematode morphotype richness and more infections per host in logged than in unlogged forest.





Leopoldamys sabanus showed higher cestode prevalence and egg counts, and higher strongylid and spirurid egg counts, in unlogged than in logged forest.





Host habitat use, diet, mobility and exposure to intermediate hosts can mediate how forest disturbance affects parasite transmission and assemblage structure.





Predictions about parasite diversity and infection under habitat disturbance should be based on the individual life histories of both hosts and parasites rather than assuming a uniform response.





Broader comparative research across more host species is needed to determine whether general patterns emerge in parasite responses to anthropogenic habitat disturbance.

title: Is Rattus rattus invading the primary rainforest on Borneo?
text:
Research article

Is Rattus rattus invading the primary rainforest on Borneo?


Konstans Wells, Dieter Kock, Maklarin B. Lakim, Martin Pfeiffer


Full citation

Wells, K., Kock, D., Lakim, M. B., & Pfeiffer, M. (2006). Is Rattus rattus invading the primary rainforest on Borneo? Malayan Nature Journal, 59, 73–79.




About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The publication combines intensive live trapping with morphological and cranial examination to document possible early-stage intrusion of an invasive commensal rat into intact rainforest. The rarity and immature age of the specimens prevent confirmation of established populations, while their occurrence far from forest edges shows that primary forest is not necessarily impermeable to Rattus dispersal.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Two specimens identified as Rattus rattus sensu lato were captured inside primary dipterocarp rainforest at Danum Valley and Tawau Hills in Sabah, Borneo.





The Danum Valley specimen was captured approximately 1.2 kilometres inside primary rainforest, and the Tawau Hills specimen approximately 0.7 kilometres inside primary rainforest.





More than 42,000 ground-trap nights and 5,000 canopy-trap nights across primary and secondary forest sites yielded only two such specimens, indicating very low apparent occurrence in the sampled primary forests.





Morphological and cranial comparisons supported assignment of the two Bornean specimens to Rattus rattus sensu lato, while uncertainty remained over separation from the Asian form Rattus tanezumi.





The immature age and low capture frequency of the specimens were consistent with either dispersing individuals or an early invasion stage, rather than established abundant populations.





The two records occurred in forests with contrasting surrounding landscapes, including an extensively forested matrix at Danum Valley and plantation-dominated surroundings at Tawau Hills.





Even low-density incursions of invasive rats into intact rainforest may pose ecological risks through competition with native small mammals, resource use and transmission of diseases or parasites.





Early detection, taxonomic clarification and continued monitoring are required to determine whether Rattus populations are becoming established in Borneo's primary rainforests.

title: Viverrid and herpestid observations by camera and small mammal cage trapping in the lowland rainforests on Borneo including a record of the Hose’s Civet, Diplogale hosei
text:
Research article

Viverrid and herpestid observations by camera and small mammal cage trapping in the lowland rainforests on Borneo including a record of the Hose’s Civet, Diplogale hosei


Konstans Wells, Alim Biun, Marius Gabin


Full citation

Wells, K., Biun, A., & Gabin, M. (2005). Viverrid and herpestid observations by camera and small mammal cage trapping in the lowland rainforests on Borneo including a record of the Hose’s Civet, Diplogale hosei. Small Carnivore Conservation, 32, 12-14.




About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The publication provides occurrence data for an elusive Bornean small-carnivore assemblage and demonstrates that camera traps and cage traps recover different species subsets. The Hose’s Civet record at approximately 600 m contributes to evidence that this poorly known species is not restricted to montane forest. The authors emphasise that sparse detections, non-target trap design and rainforest heterogeneity constrain inventories and motivate multi-method, multi-stratum survey designs.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






A camera trap recorded Hose’s Civet (Diplogale hosei) in primary lowland rainforest at approximately 600 m elevation near Poring Hot Spring in Mount Kinabalu National Park, Sabah.





Approximately 100 camera nights produced 335 wildlife photographs, of which eight photographs represented four viverrid or herpestid species: Hose’s Civet, Banded Palm Civet, Banded Linsang and Collared Mongoose.





More than 42,000 terrestrial and 1,800 arboreal cage-trap nights yielded 12 individual civets in 27 captures, representing Small-toothed Palm Civet, Common Palm Civet and Malay Civet.





All live-trapped civets were captured in the primary forests of Danum Valley and Tawau Hills National Park, while no viverrids were captured in the sampled secondary forests.





Camera trapping and small-mammal cage trapping detected different subsets of the small-carnivore assemblage, demonstrating that low encounter rates and method-specific biases can produce incomplete species inventories.





The lowland observation of Hose’s Civet adds evidence that the species’ habitat and elevational range may be broader than suggested by its predominantly montane records.





Surveys of Bornean small carnivores should account for spatial heterogeneity across local and regional scales, forest condition and vertical strata, and should combine complementary recording methods.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


No formal abstract was provided in the publication. The article reports camera-trap and small-mammal cage-trap observations of viverrids and herpestids in lowland rainforests of Sabah, Borneo. It documents a lowland record of Hose’s Civet (Diplogale hosei) at Mount Kinabalu National Park and compares species detected by camera trapping and live trapping across primary and secondary forest sites.

title: Use of arboreal and terrestrial space by a small mammal community in a tropical rain forest in Borneo, Malaysia
text:
Research article

Use of arboreal and terrestrial space by a small mammal community in a tropical rain forest in Borneo, Malaysia


Konstans Wells, Martin Pfeiffer, Maklarin B. Lakim, K. Eduard Linsenmair


Full citation

Wells, K., Pfeiffer, M., Lakim, M. B., & Linsenmair, K. E. (2004). Use of arboreal and terrestrial space by a small mammal community in a tropical rain forest in Borneo, Malaysia. Journal of Biogeography, 31(4), 641-652. https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1365-2699.2003.01032.x



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study shows that tropical small-mammal communities are vertically structured without forming sharply separated terrestrial and arboreal assemblages. Terrestrial diversity was higher, but several common species used both habitat layers. Species shared much of the available microhabitat, and differentiation arose mainly through variation in the intensity of use of tree structure, connectivity, lianas, gaps and other local habitat attributes.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Seven trapping sessions across paired terrestrial and lower-canopy grids recorded 644 captures of 118 individuals representing 20 small-mammal species from six families.





Sixteen species were recorded on the ground and 11 species in the lower canopy, with terrestrial species diversity significantly exceeding arboreal diversity.





Murid rodents dominated both habitat layers and accounted for approximately 82% of all captures.





Chiropodomys major dominated the canopy assemblage, whereas Maxomys whiteheadi and Maxomys surifer were the most abundant terrestrial species.





Niviventer cremoriventer and Tupaia minor were common in both terrestrial and arboreal traps, demonstrating that vertical habitat use formed a continuum rather than a strict ground–canopy division.





Most common small-mammal species occupied broadly overlapping portions of measured microhabitat space rather than being confined to distinct habitat types.





Tree size distribution was among the strongest fine-scale habitat correlates of capture probability for both arboreal and terrestrial species.





Branch connectivity, liana presence, canopy gaps, bark structure and crown density influenced the occurrence of particular species and local assemblages.





Microhabitat variation explained more compositional variation in terrestrial assemblages than in arboreal assemblages.





Most species pairs showed neither strong spatial avoidance nor greater-than-expected overlap in trap use.





Marked individuals showed low persistence across trapping sessions, with lower persistence in males and immature individuals than in females.





Species turnover between trapping sessions was similarly high in terrestrial and arboreal assemblages.





Ecological segregation in this small-mammal community was driven more by concentrated activity within preferred parts of broadly shared habitat than by strict habitat-layer specialization.





The structurally complex canopy may constrain foraging efficiency and thereby reduce differentiation in microhabitat use among common arboreal species.





Studies of tropical small-mammal communities should sample both ground and canopy layers because terrestrial trapping alone underrepresents vertical habitat use and arboreal diversity.





Fine-scale habitat measurements should be combined with repeated demographic sampling because local assemblages vary through both habitat associations and rapid individual turnover.

title: BAHE Research Group
text:
Research programme

BAHE investigates how interactions among organisms, environments and people shape biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, wildlife health and sustainable futures. BAHE integrates ecological observation, molecular approaches, quantitative modelling and knowledge synthesis to understand how ecological systems function across scales.



Biodiversity under Global Change
We investigate how biodiversity responds to land-use change, habitat fragmentation, urbanisation, protected areas, renewable-energy landscapes, restoration and conservation intervention.


Wildlife ecology, health and One Health
We study wildlife populations, host–parasite interactions, microbiomes, zoonotic risk and disease ecology in ecological and conservation contexts, with long-standing interests in Borneo and tropical systems.


Ecological Interactions and Dynamics
We analyse how ecological interactions and dynamic processes unfold through time, including colonisation, succession, ecological networks, biodiversity offsetting, restoration trajectories and resilience.


Nature, Wellbeing and Sustainable Futures
We explore how nature exposure, nature connectedness and ecologically mediated wellbeing can be understood within broader One Health and social–ecological sustainability frameworks.

title: BAHE Research Group
text:
How we work
BAHE uses wildlife ecology as a foundation for understanding how interactions propagate across ecological and socioecological systems. By combining field ecology, molecular ecology, quantitative modelling and interdisciplinary collaboration, we seek to explain, predict and ultimately inform responses to biodiversity loss, wildlife health, restoration and sustainable futures. We view ecological systems as interconnected networks in which understanding interactions across biological, environmental and social scales creates new opportunities for scientific discovery and evidence-based solutions.

Our approach: field ecology + biodiversity data + ecological modelling + interaction networks + interdisciplinary collaboration.

Meet BAHE






Dr Konstans Wells
Principal Investigator
BAHE is coordinated by Dr Konstans Wells at Swansea University. The group works at the interface of wildlife ecology, biodiversity science, One Health and ecological system dynamics, with long-standing interests in mammals, birds, parasites, microbiomes and tropical systems.
The group is intentionally collaborative, combining field ecology, molecular ecology, bioinformatics, quantitative modelling and systems thinking with an international network of researchers, practitioners and policy partners.

title: Join BAHE
text:
BAHE welcomes motivated researchers at different career stages who are driven by scientific curiosity, committed to rigorous ecological research and interested in understanding biodiversity, wildlife health, ecological interactions and socioecological systems in a rapidly changing world.
We particularly encourage individuals who enjoy integrating field observation, molecular and biodiversity data, conceptual thinking and quantitative analysis to address important ecological questions while contributing to biodiversity conservation, ecosystem resilience and sustainable futures.



Joining BAHE means becoming part of a collaborative, research-led environment where ecological questions drive methodological development and where field observation, biological understanding and quantitative analysis are integrated throughout the research process.
We aim to foster intellectual curiosity, scientific integrity and analytical rigour while encouraging researchers to think across disciplines and scales—from organisms and ecological interactions to ecosystems, environmental change and human wellbeing.
Researchers are encouraged to develop independence, collaborate openly and contribute to an evolving programme of research that advances both ecological understanding and evidence-based decision making.



Rather than recruiting only through advertised positions, BAHE welcomes discussions with outstanding early-career researchers interested in developing competitive fellowship applications.
We are particularly interested in researchers whose ideas align with BAHE’s interests in biodiversity, wildlife ecology, ecological interactions, One Health, quantitative ecology and sustainable futures.
Potential fellowship schemes include:

Royal Society University Research Fellowships
Royal Society Dorothy Hodgkin Fellowships
Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Fellowships
UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) fellowships
Leverhulme Early Career Fellowships
NERC Independent Research Fellowships
Wellcome Trust fellowships
Other appropriate national and international fellowship schemes

Prospective applicants are encouraged to contact us well in advance of application deadlines to discuss scientific fit, proposal development and institutional support.



BAHE welcomes prospective doctoral researchers who are excited by fundamental ecological questions and motivated to contribute to rigorous, interdisciplinary science.
Projects are normally developed collaboratively around shared scientific interests, available expertise and suitable funding opportunities rather than from predefined project lists.
Research interests currently include: - biodiversity responses to environmental change - wildlife ecology, parasites and microbiomes - ecological interactions and community assembly - One Health and disease ecology - ecological modelling and Bayesian statistics - biodiversity monitoring and evidence synthesis - restoration ecology and ecosystem resilience - nature, wellbeing and sustainable futures
Strong applicants typically demonstrate: - genuine scientific curiosity - excellent academic preparation - independent thinking and initiative - strong communication skills - quantitative, field or laboratory experience appropriate to their background - enthusiasm for interdisciplinary ecological research



The MRes provides intensive research experience within an active research environment and is an excellent pathway towards doctoral research, conservation science, quantitative ecology or related research careers.
Potential research areas include:

wildlife ecology and disease ecology
biodiversity monitoring and ecological modelling
urban ecology and One Health
tropical ecology and conservation
ecological interactions and ecological networks
microbiomes and host-associated communities
evidence synthesis and meta-analysis

Applicants commonly come from backgrounds including ecology, zoology, biology, environmental science, geography, conservation, veterinary biosciences, mathematics, statistics or data science.
For information about entry requirements, programme structure and university regulations, please see the Swansea University Biosciences MRes programme.



Subject to available capacity, BAHE welcomes enquiries from:

visiting PhD students
visiting postdoctoral researchers
undergraduate and postgraduate research placements
research interns
international visiting researchers
academic visitors interested in collaborative research

Visits are normally developed around shared research interests and ongoing projects.




Research philosophy: Curiosity about the diversity, complexity and resilience of the natural world is the starting point of scientific discovery and the motivation for understanding ecological change. BAHE integrates field observation, conceptual thinking, quantitative analysis and interdisciplinary synthesis to reveal how interactions among organisms, ecosystems and people shape biodiversity across scales. We aim to develop independent scientists who combine intellectual curiosity with analytical rigour, advancing ecological understanding while generating evidence that supports biodiversity conservation, ecosystem resilience and informed decisions for sustainable futures.







Ecological observation, biodiversity monitoring, wildlife sampling, study design and long-term ecological research.



R programming, Bayesian statistics, ecological modelling, simulation, reproducible workflows and ecological inference.



Conceptual development, hypothesis formulation, critical interpretation, evidence synthesis and interdisciplinary integration.



Scientific writing, visualisation, presentations, collaborative research, open science and knowledge exchange.



Connecting ecological understanding with biodiversity conservation, restoration, wildlife health and sustainable futures.



Developing original ideas, collaborative networks, grant writing and long-term scientific leadership.





Beyond academic achievement, we value researchers who demonstrate:

curiosity about the natural world
enthusiasm for ecological discovery
commitment to scientific excellence
integrity and openness in research
willingness to learn across disciplines
collaborative spirit
critical thinking and intellectual independence
motivation to contribute knowledge that benefits biodiversity and society




If you are interested in joining BAHE, please send a concise email including:

the type of opportunity you are interested in (Postdoctoral Fellowship, PhD, MRes, visiting researcher or placement);
a brief description of your research interests;
how your interests align with BAHE research;
relevant experience and technical skills;
information on existing or potential funding (where applicable);
a short curriculum vitae.


Strong enquiries usually demonstrate scientific curiosity, familiarity with relevant literature and a clear explanation of why BAHE provides an appropriate environment for developing the proposed research. We do not expect a complete research proposal, but we encourage applicants to identify one or two ecological questions they find particularly exciting and explain how they would like to explore them.




BAHE seeks to build a research community in which curiosity, scientific integrity and mutual respect provide the foundation for collaboration and discovery. We believe that excellent science is strengthened by diversity in people, disciplines, experiences, cultures and ideas, and that tackling complex ecological challenges requires openness to different perspectives and ways of thinking. We welcome talented researchers from all backgrounds who share a commitment to rigorous, collaborative and inclusive research.
Contact us

title: Publications
text: This collection presents selected peer-reviewed publications from the BAHE Knowledge Network. Each publication is accompanied by curated summaries, knowledge statements and links to related media and research resources to allow exploring both the publication and its broader scientific context. We welcome constructive discussion, collaboration and feedback that support ecological research and the continued development of the BAHE Knowledge Network.

title: Publications
text:
Featured publications




Biodiversity offsetting Ecological compensation Habitat succession Colonization dynamics



 Featured publication
Research article

Optimizing biodiversity offsetting for habitat succession and colonization dynamics

Konstans Wells, Luca Börger, Miguel Lurgi, Kevin Watts, James M. Bullock


Conservation Biology · 2026


This study provides a quantitative ecological framework for improving biodiversity offset policy by demonstrating that robust no-net-loss outcomes require larger compensation areas, long-term habitat protection and explicit incorporation of ecological recovery, succession and landscape dynamics into offset design.

Diversity and Plasticity in Mosquito Feeding Patterns: A Meta-Analysis of 'Universal' DNA Diet Studies

Meshach Lee, Richard O'Rorke, Nicholas J. Clark, Tamsyn Uren Webster, Konstans Wells


Global Ecology and Biogeography 34(6), e70077 · 2025


This global synthesis demonstrates that assumptions of narrow or fixed mosquito host preferences can underestimate the breadth and flexibility of vector-host interactions. Its findings support more dynamic approaches to modelling mosquito-borne disease risk under environmental change.

Alessandra Giacomini, Maklarin B. Lakim, Fred Y. Y. Tuh, Matthew Hitchings, Sofia Consuegra, Tamsyn Uren Webster, Konstans Wells


Molecular Ecology 34(11) · 2025


The findings show that urbanisation can reshape wildlife gut microbiomes in host-specific ways and that ecological niche overlap may partially override phylogenetic expectations among co-occurring native and invasive species.

title: Arboreal spacing patterns of the large pencil-tailed tree mouse, Chiropodomys major (Muridae), in a rainforest in Sabah, Malaysia
text:
Research article

Arboreal spacing patterns of the large pencil-tailed tree mouse, Chiropodomys major (Muridae), in a rainforest in Sabah, Malaysia


Konstans Wells, Martin Pfeiffer, Maklarin Bin Lakim, Karl Eduard Linsenmair


Full citation

Wells, K., Pfeiffer, M., Lakim, M. B., & Linsenmair, K. E. (2004). Arboreal spacing patterns of the large pencil-tailed tree mouse, Chiropodomys major (Muridae), in a rainforest in Sabah, Malaysia. Ecotropica, 10(1), 15-22.



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study provides one of the first quantitative descriptions of spacing in a small arboreal tropical rodent. Males occupied larger ranges than females, but ranges of both sexes overlapped broadly, arguing against territoriality. The species used nearly all sampled arboreal habitat and was associated particularly with lianas and canopy gaps.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Chiropodomys major was the most frequently captured small-mammal species in the sampled subcanopy, with 275 captures of 40 individuals.





Only two individuals of Chiropodomys major were captured in ground traps, confirming that the species was predominantly arboreal at the study site.





Home-range estimates were calculated for 18 resident individuals with at least five captures using 90 percent core convex polygons.





Male Chiropodomys major had significantly larger home ranges than females, averaging approximately 2,971 square metres compared with 1,580 square metres.





Male home ranges varied from about 1,600 to 4,600 square metres, whereas female ranges varied from about 200 to 2,600 square metres.





Home ranges of both sexes overlapped with those of same-sex and opposite-sex individuals, indicating that exclusive territories were not maintained.





Male home ranges overlapped with more same-sex individuals than female home ranges did.





Adult individuals persisted in the study area for longer than immature individuals.





Chiropodomys major was recorded at 56 of 62 arboreal trap stations, demonstrating use of nearly the entire sampled subcanopy habitat.





Capture frequency was positively associated with the presence of canopy gaps and lianas.





Trap height was not correlated with the number of captured individuals or total captures.





Some individuals used nesting or refuge sites near the ground, including tree hollows, dead stumps and holes near roots or logs.





The broad overlap of adult ranges is consistent with a nonterritorial spacing system and permits a promiscuous mating structure.





Scattered and unpredictable canopy resources may make exclusive territorial defence inefficient for Chiropodomys major.





Branch connections, lianas and the ability to descend through vegetation likely facilitate agile movement through the structurally heterogeneous canopy.





More extensive telemetry and year-round sampling are needed to quantify three-dimensional home ranges, seasonal changes and vertical space use in arboreal small mammals.

title: Eat in or take away – seed predation and removal by rats (Muridae) during a fruiting event in a dipterocarp rainforest
text:
Research article

Eat in or take away – seed predation and removal by rats (Muridae) during a fruiting event in a dipterocarp rainforest


Konstans Wells, Robert Bagchi


Full citation

Wells, K., & Bagchi, R. (2005). Eat in or take away – seed predation and removal by rats (Muridae) during a fruiting event in a dipterocarp rainforest. The Raffles Bulletin of Zoology, 53(2), 281-286.




About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Seed predation, seed removal and forest regeneration during a Bornean mast-fruiting event. Clockwise from upper left: fruits of the stone oak Lithocarpus sp.; the spectacular rain of dipterocarp seeds during a mast-fruiting event in Danum Valley Conservation Area; newly germinated dipterocarp seedlings emerging after seed fall; a spool-line experiment showing a seed removed into the concealed burrow of a spiny rat (Maxomys rajah/M. surifer), whose entrance was sealed with leaf litter after the animal entered; and a Whitehead's spiny rat (Maxomys whiteheadi) consuming a fresh dipterocarp seed. Together, these images illustrate how tropical forest rodents influence seed fate through predation, transport and temporary storage, processes that can simultaneously reduce seed survival while contributing to secondary seed dispersal and subsequent forest regeneration. Credit: Konstans Wells




Research overview


The study demonstrates that Bornean rats are important consumers of both dipterocarp and stone-oak seeds, but seed removal does not always lead to immediate destruction. Transport to burrows, burial of Lithocarpus seeds, long handling times and survival of some partially eaten seeds create pathways through which rats may also contribute to secondary dispersal.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Rats exploited Parashorea malaanonan and Lithocarpus gracilis seeds at similar frequencies during a partial fruiting event in lowland dipterocarp rainforest.





Nine of 55 Parashorea malaanonan seeds and 11 of 55 Lithocarpus gracilis seeds were exploited at experimental feeding stations.





Most exploited seeds were removed from their feeding stations rather than consumed at the point of encounter.





Seeds placed near Maxomys rajah burrows were moved into the burrows, demonstrating directed transport to protected locations.





Lithocarpus gracilis seeds were more frequently displaced than Parashorea malaanonan seeds, and two displaced Lithocarpus seeds were found buried.





Eight percent of Parashorea malaanonan seeds collected in seed traps showed rodent damage, indicating that seed exploitation also occurred in the canopy.





Some partially consumed Parashorea malaanonan seeds retained the capacity to germinate.





Captive Maxomys rats consumed several dipterocarp and other hard-shelled seed species but rejected the tested Ficus, Aglaia and Tetrastigma fruits.





Feeding on a single Parashorea malaanonan seed lasted for as long as 27 minutes.





Captive rats commonly moved seeds before feeding and sometimes concealed Lithocarpus gracilis seeds under leaves or in cage corners.





Rat capture rates declined significantly during the fruiting period, whereas capture rates of tree shrews and civets did not show the same decline.





Reduced rat trap success during fruiting is consistent with abundant natural seeds reducing attraction to banana-baited traps.





Rapidly germinating dipterocarp seeds are more likely to be moved for protected consumption, whereas slowly germinating Lithocarpus seeds are more suitable for caching.





Rats can function simultaneously as seed predators and secondary seed dispersers because they transport seeds, cache some seeds and may leave partially consumed seeds viable.





Rodent seed exploitation extends across forest strata and may operate over longer periods through caching than seed predation by larger, more mobile mammals.





Future studies should track removed seeds to their final fate and quantify caching, seed survival and seedling recruitment under contrasting levels of forest disturbance.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Seed predators are considered important in the evolution of mast fruiting. Mast events in turn provide an abundant food resource for consumers, but only for a limited period of time. In this study seed removal experiments, feeding trials and small mammal trapping were used to determine the potential of forest rats (Muridae) as predators and dispersers of two tree species, Lithocarpus gracilis (Fagaceae) and Parashorea malaanonan (Dipterocarpaceae) during a minor fruiting event in a dipterocarp rainforest at Danum Valley (Sabah, Malaysia) in Sept/Oct 2004. Seeds of both species were exploited by rodents at similar frequencies. Nearly all seeds exploited were removed from the feeding stations. Seeds placed near burrows of Maxomys rajah were moved into the burrows. Gnawed seeds collected in fruit fall traps (8% of total collected) indicated that Parashorea seeds were also exploited in the canopy. Partially eaten seeds often retained their ability to germinate. Captive rats ate a range of dipterocarp and other hard-shelled seed and feeding on an individual seed could take up to 27 minutes. Trap success for rats, but not tree shrews (Tupaiidae) and civets (Viverridae), decreased during the fruiting season. This supports the idea that this group benefits from mast fruiting. Rats are evidently important predators of the seeds of these tree species, both before and after dispersal. However, due to the removal of seeds before eating, long consumption times and the ability of partially consumed seeds to germinate, they may also function as secondary dispersal agents.

title: Movement trajectories and habitat partitioning of small mammals in logged and unlogged rain forests on Borneo
text:
Research article

Movement trajectories and habitat partitioning of small mammals in logged and unlogged rain forests on Borneo


Konstans Wells, Martin Pfeiffer, Maklarin B. Lakim, Elisabeth K. V. Kalko


Full citation

Wells, K., Pfeiffer, M., Lakim, M. B., & Kalko, E. K. V. (2006). Movement trajectories and habitat partitioning of small mammals in logged and unlogged rain forests on Borneo. Journal of Animal Ecology, 75(5), 1212-1223. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2656.2006.01144.x



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Movement and habitat partitioning of eight small-mammal species in Bornean rain forest. Species differed in vertical activity and substrate use, while comparison of logged and unlogged forests showed species-specific shifts rather than a uniform response to forest disturbance. Congeneric species with similar morphology often occupied nearby regions of multivariate movement space but changed in contrasting directions after logging. Credit: Wells et al. (2006)




Research overview


The study demonstrates that fine-scale movement trajectories reveal ecological differentiation not captured by trapping records alone. Species segregated along gradients of vertical activity, support use and undergrowth structure, with morphology contributing more strongly than body size to climbing behaviour. Logging changed movement in every focal species, but responses were idiosyncratic and did not alter the shared underlying strategy of short, tortuous movement through heterogeneous forest habitat.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Spool-and-line tracking produced 212 movement tracks totalling 13,525 metres from at least 188 individuals of eight small-mammal species in Borneo.





Movement trajectories differed significantly among species in climbing activity, above-ground movement, maximum height, support use, undergrowth use, step length and turning angle.





Congeneric species with similar body size and morphology, including Maxomys rajah and Maxomys surifer and Tupaia longipes and Tupaia tana, showed the strongest similarities in movement and habitat use.





Principal component analysis identified above-ground activity as the dominant axis of interspecific movement differentiation, explaining 54% of total variation.





Body mass was positively associated with step length but not with climbing activity or the diameter of supportive structures used.





Relative hind-foot and tail dimensions were associated with above-ground movement and support use, indicating that morphology rather than body size alone structures vertical habitat exploitation.





All focal species changed at least some aspects of their movement trajectories between logged and unlogged forests.





Leopoldamys sabanus exhibited the largest number of movement changes between forest types, including shifts in above-ground activity, log use, support diameter, undergrowth use, step length and turning angle.





Tupaia longipes and Leopoldamys sabanus increased above-ground movement in logged forest, whereas Maxomys rajah reduced above-ground activity.





Species pairs with similar morphology changed in contrasting directions between logged and unlogged forest, showing that convergent body form did not produce uniform disturbance responses.





The frequency distributions of step lengths and overall path tortuosity were similar between logged and unlogged forests despite significant changes in specific habitat-use variables.





The prevalence of short steps and stable path tortuosity across species and forest types indicates movement adapted to heterogeneous habitat rather than simple random-walk behaviour.





Bornean small mammals can be partitioned into terrestrial, scansorial and arboreal movement guilds, but these categories form a continuum rather than a strict ground–canopy dichotomy.





Forest logging alters the structural context of movement but does not necessarily replace the fundamental small-scale movement strategy used by a species.





Movement ecology studies of tropical small mammals should measure both trajectory geometry and the structural substrates used along paths rather than relying solely on trapping locations.





Species-specific responses to altered forest structure limit the reliability of broad functional-group generalisations for predicting persistence in logged tropical forests.

title: Effects of rain forest logging on species richness and assemblage composition of small mammals in Southeast Asia
text:
Research article

Effects of rain forest logging on species richness and assemblage composition of small mammals in Southeast Asia


Konstans Wells, Elisabeth K. V. Kalko, Maklarin B. Lakim, Martin Pfeiffer


Full citation

Wells, K., Kalko, E. K. V., Lakim, M. B., & Pfeiffer, M. (2007). Effects of rain forest logging on species richness and assemblage composition of small mammals in Southeast Asia. Journal of Biogeography, 34(6), 1087-1099. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2699.2006.01677.x



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Diversity and assemblage structure of small non-volant mammals in three unlogged and three logged forests in Sabah. Species-accumulation curves show substantially greater richness in unlogged forests, whereas rank-abundance distributions and ordination patterns indicate that common-species dominance and overall assemblage dynamics remained comparatively similar between forest types. Credit: Wells et al. (2007)




Research overview


The study shows that logging strongly reduces small-mammal species richness by disproportionately affecting rare, endemic, arboreal and specialised taxa, while leaving many common murids and tree shrews comparatively resilient. Similar dominance and abundance dynamics across forest types demonstrate that community-level stability can coexist with substantial biodiversity loss.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Two years of trapping across six Bornean forest sites recorded 1,218 individuals representing 28 species of small non-volant mammals.





Unlogged forests supported 27 recorded species, whereas logged forests supported 17 species.





Estimated species richness was consistently higher in unlogged forests than in logged forests across Chao2, first-order jackknife and rarefaction analyses.





The difference in richness between forest types was driven primarily by the loss or reduced detection of rare species rather than by the disappearance of common species.





Eleven common species accounted for approximately 95% of all captures and nearly all occurred in both logged and unlogged forests.





Overall Shannon diversity was lower in logged forests even though single-site diversity estimates did not differ consistently between forest types.





Dominance patterns, rank-abundance distributions and fluctuations in common-species abundance were broadly similar between logged and unlogged forests.





Niviventer cremoriventer and Tupaia tana were significantly more abundant in logged forests than in unlogged forests.





Local and regional changes in small-mammal assemblage structure were strongly correlated, indicating similar ecological patterns across spatial scales.





Murid and tupaiid assemblages showed correlated fluctuations in space and time, suggesting partial responses to shared environmental drivers.





Geographic distance among forest sites explained more variation in assemblage similarity than seasonal or chronological differences among trapping sessions.





Rare endemic, arboreal and more specialised mammals were disproportionately absent or reduced in logged forest.





Logged forests retained a large proportion of the common small-mammal fauna found in unlogged forests and therefore have substantial conservation value.





Community-level stability in common species can mask substantial biodiversity loss among rare and specialised taxa.





Assessments of logging effects should combine replicated sites, multi-year sampling and both local and regional analyses to distinguish habitat effects from spatial heterogeneity.





Conservation planning in production landscapes should protect remaining unlogged forests while recognising logged forests as important secondary habitat for disturbance-tolerant species.

title: Superb fairy-wren males aggregate into hidden leks to solicit extragroup fertilizations before dawn
text:
Research article

Superb fairy-wren males aggregate into hidden leks to solicit extragroup fertilizations before dawn


Andrew Cockburn, Anastasia H. Dalziell, Caroline J. Blackmore, Michael C. Double, Hanna Kokko, Helen L. Osmond, Nadeena R. Beck, Megan L. Head, Konstans Wells


Full citation

Cockburn, A., Dalziell, A. H., Blackmore, C. J., Double, M. C., Kokko, H., Osmond, H. L., Beck, N. R., Head, M. L., & Wells, K. (2009). Superb fairy-wren males aggregate into hidden leks to solicit extragroup fertilizations before dawn. Behavioral Ecology, 20(3), 501–510. https://doi.org/10.1093/beheco/arp024



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study extends hidden-lek theory to a cooperatively breeding bird with year-round all-purpose territories. Males clustered their dawn-song posts, shared local dialects and competed intensely for access to females making predawn fertilization forays. Subordinates and neighbours gained paternity by acting as satellites around attractive early-moulting males.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Male superb fairy-wrens began increasing dawn-song advertisement at the same time of year regardless of social status, plumage timing or presumed quality.





Dawn song posts were more spatially clustered than expected under random placement within year-round territories.





Males within spatial song clusters generally used the same distinctive trill-song dialect during the dawn chorus, despite many males being able to sing several dialects.





Subordinate males sang close to dominant males or occupied dominant song perches despite repeated attacks and displacement by dominants.





Female superb fairy-wrens repeatedly visited the same male cluster across a breeding season when seeking extragroup fertilizations.





Most extragroup offspring were sired by males from the same local song cluster, and preferred early-moulting males lost substantial paternity to subordinate males and immediate neighbours.





The spatial aggregation of advertising males is consistent with a hidden lek in which lower-quality satellite males exploit proximity to highly attractive males.





Satellite behaviour by subordinate and neighbouring males provides a mechanism through which competitive male aggregation can generate multiple extragroup paternity and avian polyandry.

title: Ectoparasite Infestations of Hedgehogs (Erinaceus europaeus) are Associated with Small-Scale Landscape Structures in an Urban–Suburban Environment
text:
Research article

Ectoparasite Infestations of Hedgehogs (Erinaceus europaeus) are Associated with Small-Scale Landscape Structures in an Urban–Suburban Environment


Sven Thamm, Elisabeth K. V. Kalko, Konstans Wells


Full citation

Thamm, S., Kalko, E. K. V., & Wells, K. (2009). Ectoparasite Infestations of Hedgehogs (Erinaceus europaeus) are Associated with Small-Scale Landscape Structures in an Urban–Suburban Environment. EcoHealth, 6(3), 404-413. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10393-009-0268-3



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Urban–suburban landscape context of hedgehog sampling around Ulm, southwestern Germany. Capture locations were embedded within a fine-grained mosaic of built-up land, roads, arable fields, grassland and forest. Landscape composition and heterogeneity were quantified within 20, 50 and 100 metre buffers to test their associations with flea and tick burdens. Credit: Thamm, Kalko and Wells (2009)




Research overview


The study demonstrates that parasite burdens can respond to landscape structure at spatial scales comparable to individual host movement. Flea burdens were lower in more heterogeneous landscapes and where road coverage was greater, whereas tick burdens were associated with arable, built-up and road features and with seasonal timing. These results connect urban landscape ecology, host movement and parasite acquisition at the individual level.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Fleas were recorded on 50 of 56 European hedgehogs sampled across the urban–suburban study landscape.





The flea Archeopsylla erinacei reached burdens of up to 100 individuals per hedgehog, with 907 fleas collected in total.





Tick infestations were recorded on 49 of 56 hedgehogs, including both Ixodes hexagonus and Ixodes ricinus.





Of the identified ticks, approximately 65% were Ixodes hexagonus and 35% were Ixodes ricinus.





Flea burdens declined as land-cover diversity and heterogeneity increased within 50 and 100 metre buffers around hedgehog capture locations.





Greater road coverage within 50 and 100 metre buffers was associated with lower flea burdens on hedgehogs.





Patch richness and the Shannon diversity of patch numbers within 20 metres were negatively associated with flea burden but had less explanatory power than landscape variables measured at 50 and 100 metres.





Tick infestation levels declined with increasing arable land cover and with increasing numbers of arable patches across the analysed spatial scales.





Tick infestation increased with built-up land cover within 50 and 100 metre buffers and with the number of roads within 50 metres.





Tick infestation intensity declined through the April-to-August sampling period.





Flea and tick burdens were not correlated with geographic distance among hedgehog capture locations.





Residual variograms showed little evidence of spatial autocorrelation after landscape variables were included in the infestation models.





Small-scale landscape heterogeneity can influence parasite acquisition by neighbouring hosts even when infestation patterns show no simple spatial clustering.





Flea burdens may respond indirectly to landscape structure through effects on hedgehog movement, aggregation, density and use of resting sites.





Tick responses to built-up and arable land should be interpreted cautiously because Ixodes hexagonus and Ixodes ricinus differ substantially in off-host ecology and questing strategy.





Host–parasite models in urban environments should incorporate fine-scale landscape composition and heterogeneity rather than assuming homogeneous habitat matrices.

title: Top-down control of herbivory by birds and bats in the canopy of temperate broad-leaved oaks (Quercus robur)
text:
Research article

Top-down control of herbivory by birds and bats in the canopy of temperate broad-leaved oaks (Quercus robur)


Stefan M. Böhm, Konstans Wells, Elisabeth K. V. Kalko


Full citation

Böhm, S. M., Wells, K., & Kalko, E. K. V. (2011). Top-Down Control of Herbivory by Birds and Bats in the Canopy of Temperate Broad-Leaved Oaks (Quercus robur). PLOS ONE, 6(4), e17857. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0017857



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Differences in mean damage of leaf area (A) and mean number of holes (B) per leaf for exclusions (shaded bars) and controls (open bars) at the two study sites and for young and mature oaks on the Schwäbische Alb. Significant differences in variables are indicated by “*”. Error bars indicate one SE; variables are presented as square-root transformed values.. Credit: Böhm, Wells and Kalko (2011)




Research overview


The study provides experimental evidence for a trophic cascade in temperate forest canopies. Birds and bats suppress herbivorous arthropods, thereby reducing damage to Quercus robur leaves. The magnitude of this ecosystem service varies with tree age, stand composition and regional predator diversity, linking biodiversity directly to forest function.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Excluding birds and bats from Quercus robur crowns significantly increased both leaf-area damage and the number of arthropod feeding holes.





On young oaks in the Schwäbische Alb, vertebrate exclusion increased mean leaf-area damage by approximately 40% and the number of holes per leaf by approximately 29%.





On mature oaks, vertebrate exclusion increased mean leaf-area damage by approximately 23% in the Schwäbische Alb and 44% in Hainich-Dün.





On mature oaks, vertebrate exclusion increased the number of feeding holes per leaf by approximately 16% in the Schwäbische Alb and 39% in Hainich-Dün.





Leaf damage was greater on young than on mature oaks in the Schwäbische Alb, indicating that tree age modifies herbivory and predator effects.





Mature oaks in the Schwäbische Alb experienced substantially greater herbivory than mature oaks in Hainich-Dün.





Higher bird species richness, higher bird abundance and greater foliage-gleaning bat activity in Hainich-Dün coincided with lower herbivory than in the Schwäbische Alb.





Birds and bats provide a measurable ecosystem service by suppressing herbivorous arthropods and reducing canopy leaf damage in temperate oak forests.





The strength of top-down herbivory control depends on local forest composition, tree age and the richness and abundance of vertebrate predators.





Exclosure experiments combined with repeated phytometric measurements can quantify cascading effects of vertebrate predation on herbivory in forest canopies.





Declines in insectivorous bird and bat diversity may increase arthropod herbivory and reduce forest productivity.





Forest management should retain structurally diverse stands, dead wood, oaks, cavity-bearing trees and refuge habitats that support insectivorous birds and bats.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


The intensive foraging of insectivorous birds and bats is well known to reduce the density of arboreal herbivorous arthropods but quantification of collateral leaf damage remains limited for temperate forest canopies. We conducted exclusion experiments with nets in the crowns of young and mature oaks, Quercus robur, in south and central Germany to investigate the extent to which aerial vertebrates reduce herbivory through predation. We repeatedly estimated leaf damage throughout the vegetation period. Exclusion of birds and bats led to a distinct increase in arthropod herbivory, emphasizing the prominent role of vertebrate predators in controlling arthropods. Leaf damage (e.g., number of holes) differed strongly between sites and was 59% higher in south Germany, where species richness of vertebrate predators and relative oak density were lower compared with our other study site in central Germany. The effects of bird and bat exclusion on herbivory were 19% greater on young than on mature trees in south Germany. Our results support previous studies that have demonstrated clear effects of insectivorous vertebrates on leaf damage through the control of herbivorous arthropods. Moreover, our comparative approach on quantification of leaf damage highlights the importance of local attributes such as tree age, forest composition and species richness of vertebrate predators for control of arthropod herbivory.

title: Local and landscape-scale forest attributes differ in their impact on bird assemblages across years in forest production landscapes
text:
Research article

Local and landscape-scale forest attributes differ in their impact on bird assemblages across years in forest production landscapes


Konstans Wells, Stefan M. Böhm, Steffen Boch, Markus Fischer, Elisabeth K. V. Kalko


Full citation

Wells, K., Böhm, S. M., Boch, S., Fischer, M., & Kalko, E. K. V. (2011). Local and landscape-scale forest attributes differ in their impact on bird assemblages across years in forest production landscapes. Basic and Applied Ecology, 12(2), 97-106. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.baae.2011.01.002



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study shows that bird assemblage responses to managed forest structure are both scale dependent and temporally unstable. Landscape compositional heterogeneity best explained richness in one year, whereas local stand age and succession stage were more important in the next. Young stands also supported greater temporal turnover, linking forest development stage to dynamic occupancy processes.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Estimated regional bird species richness declined from 28 species in 2008 to 22 species in 2009, demonstrating substantial annual fluctuation in the regional species pool.





Most bird species occupied fewer forest plots in 2009 than in 2008.





Bird species turnover between years declined significantly with forest stand age.





Species turnover was significantly higher in thicket and pole-wood stands than in young and old timber stands.





Stand-area heterogeneity within an 800-metre radius was the strongest predictor of bird species richness in 2008.





Local stand succession stage and stand age were the most influential predictors of bird species richness in 2009.





The scale at which landscape variables correlated with species richness differed among variables and between years.





Landscape-scale conclusions based on only two or three arbitrarily selected spatial extents can be unreliable because nearby scales are strongly collinear and variable importance changes continuously with scale.





Hierarchical multi-species occupancy models can estimate species richness and turnover while accounting jointly for imperfect detection and unobserved species.





Short-term studies can produce non-transferable species–habitat relationships when the relative importance of local and landscape forest attributes changes between years.





Compositional heterogeneity among managed forest stands may partly buffer the loss of structural complexity within individual production stands.





Sustainable forest management should integrate local stand characteristics, landscape heterogeneity and multi-year variation in bird occupancy.

It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The publication provides a reproducible framework for reducing multiple, partly correlated grassland-management inputs to a single quantitative gradient. It shows that the compound index captures variation in plant and soil indicators across heterogeneous management systems while retaining a transparent link to mowing, grazing and fertilization. The study also demonstrates that multi-year averaging is important because management practices vary substantially among years.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






The proposed land-use intensity index integrates fertilization, mowing frequency and livestock grazing intensity into a single continuous, dimensionless measure for managed grasslands.





Each land-use component is standardized relative to its regional mean before the three components are added, allowing comparison among sites with different combinations of grassland management.





Across up to 150 grassland plots in three German regions, the compound land-use intensity index significantly predicted the first principal component of five plant and soil response variables.





Vascular plant diversity declined significantly with increasing land-use intensity in the Schwäbische Alb and Hainich regions.





Fertilization and mowing intensities were positively correlated, whereas grazing intensity was negatively related to fertilization and mowing, illustrating why categorical or single-component measures can confound grassland management effects.





Interannual variation in management, particularly grazing, made the choice of reference year or multi-year averaging more influential than the specific standardization method used to calculate the index.





The compound index is intended as a common baseline for testing general responses to land-use intensity and should be complemented by analyses of individual management components for mechanistic interpretation.

Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The paper shows that broad acidobacterial subgroups conceal ecologically distinct populations. Soil chemistry, moisture, plant diversity and soil nanofauna affected community composition, but populations within the same subgroup often responded in opposite directions.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Acidobacterial communities differed significantly between grassland and forest soils and among the three German study regions.





Grassland soils were dominated by Acidobacteria subgroup Gp6, whereas forest soils were dominated by subgroup Gp1.





Soil pH was the strongest overall predictor of acidobacterial community composition, with additional effects of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, ammonium, moisture and C-to-N ratio.





Land-use type had little direct influence compared with soil properties, although grassland and forest environments supported distinct communities.





Populations within the same acidobacterial subgroup showed contrasting correlations with the same environmental variable.





Clone-sequence analysis revealed relationships with vascular plant diversity and soil protozoa that were not apparent from subgroup-level fingerprinting alone.





Some Acidobacteria populations were associated with nutrient-poor soils, whereas others were most abundant under nutrient-rich conditions.





Ecological analyses of Acidobacteria should resolve individual populations below the subgroup level to avoid masking divergent responses.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


In soil, Acidobacteria constitute on average 20% of all bacteria, are highly diverse, and are physiologically active in situ. However, their individual functions and interactions with higher taxa in soil are still unknown. Here, potential effects of land use, soil properties, plant diversity, and soil nanofauna on acidobacterial community composition were studied by cultivation-independent methods in grassland and forest soils from three different regions in Germany. The analysis of 16S rRNA gene clone libraries representing all studied soils revealed that grassland soils were dominated by subgroup Gp6 and forest soils by subgroup Gp1 Acidobacteria. The analysis of a large number of sites (n = 57) by 16S rRNA gene fingerprinting methods showed that Acidobacteria diversity differed between grassland and forest soils and among regions. Edaphic properties affected community composition, but correlations among populations within the same subgroup differed, showing that ecological responses must be assessed below the subgroup level.

Trait-dependent occupancy dynamics of birds in temperate forest landscapes: fine-scale observations in a hierarchical multi-species framework
