It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study integrates fine-scale environmental variation with trait-based community ecology in a single occupancy framework. Although forest type and stand development explained modest proportions of total assemblage variation, species-specific responses were substantial. Body mass, breeding-range limits and spring arrival structured regional occupancy, while breeding and foraging strata varied more strongly across plots and years, linking local forest structure to functional community responses.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Bird species richness and year-to-year changes in regional prevalence differed among the Swabian Alb, Hainich and Schorfheide forest regions.





Forest type and forest successional stage each explained approximately 3–5% of assemblage-level variation in bird occurrence probability, while distance to forest edge explained less than 1%.





Species-level responses to forest type and stand development were evident even though forest management variables explained a relatively small share of total assemblage-level variation.





Ecological traits explained between approximately 16% and 83% of variation in assemblage-level bird occurrence probability across the three regions.





Bird occurrence probability declined by approximately 13% for every 100 g increase in body mass across all three regions.





Species with more northerly southern breeding-range limits had lower occurrence probabilities, especially in the Swabian Alb.





Later spring arrival was associated with lower occurrence probability, with the strongest effect in the Hainich region.





Effects of breeding strata, foraging strata, diet and phylogenetic order varied among years and forest plots, showing that trait–occupancy relationships are context dependent.





Traits linked to local resource use and vertical forest structure were more informative for fine-scale occupancy variation than broad life-history traits alone.





Hierarchical multi-species occupancy models can jointly estimate detectability, species richness, environmental responses and trait-dependent assemblage patterns while borrowing information across species.





Conservation strategies optimised for one forest region may not transfer directly to another because ecological trait effects and occupancy responses vary regionally.





Maintaining tree-species diversity, structural heterogeneity, old trees and dead wood within managed stands can help buffer adverse effects of silviculture on bird communities.

About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The publication demonstrates that fertilization, mowing and grazing do not operate as independent, spatially uniform drivers of grassland plant diversity. Fertilization produced the strongest overall reductions in richness, grazing effects depended strongly on livestock type, and all major responses were modified by interactions with land-use type and region. Environmental covariates further explained substantial variation among sites.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Across 1,514 grassland plots in three German regions, fertilization was associated with a 15% reduction in vascular plant species richness and a 0.1-unit reduction in Shannon diversity at the 16 m² plot scale.





Fertilization reduced the proportion of herb species and increased the proportion of grass species, indicating systematic shifts in plant functional-group composition.





Grazing had the second largest overall association with plant diversity, whereas mowing showed the smallest overall effects among the principal land-use components examined.





Sheep-grazed grasslands had higher-than-average vascular plant richness, whereas cattle-grazed grasslands had substantially lower richness.





The effects of fertilization depended on grassland type and region, with significant interactions among fertilization, meadow or pasture use and regional context.





Abandoned grasslands differed from managed grasslands in region-specific ways, with plant richness increasing in Hainich-Dün but decreasing slightly in Schorfheide-Chorin.





Soil type, elevation and slope significantly influenced plant diversity and composition and were necessary covariates for separating management effects from environmental site differences.





Grassland management recommendations should not be transferred uncritically among regions because the magnitude and sometimes direction of land-use effects depend on regional environmental and management context.

Model-based tick–mammal interaction probabilities and inferred host ranges in Bornean forests. The heat map shows posterior infestation probabilities for each tick–host combination, while the accompanying distributions demonstrate how limited field sampling can underestimate the number of host species used by ticks. Under exhaustive sampling, all focal tick species were predicted to infest broad and similar host ranges. Credit: Wells et al. (2013)




Research overview


The study demonstrates that apparent host specificity can emerge from uneven sampling rather than true biological specialisation. Host identity and local abundance dominated variation in infestation probability, whereas environmental covariates had weak effects. By modelling individual encounters and propagating uncertainty to species-level network indices, the analysis revealed that all focal tick species were broad host generalists.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Thirteen hard tick species were recorded from 37 mammalian host species in Bornean forests, with ticks detected on 237 of 1,444 examined host individuals.





Host species identity explained approximately 75% of variation in tick infestation probability, whereas tick species identity explained only about 4%.





Local host abundance explained an additional 8–10% of variation in infestation probability and was positively associated with tick occurrence.





Leopoldamys sabanus, Maxomys rajah, Maxomys alticola, Tupaia longipes and Tupaia gracilis had the highest estimated infestation probabilities among sampled mammals.





Forest type, sampling site, host body mass, habitat use, year and month had comparatively little explanatory power for infestation probability.





Observed interaction matrices substantially underestimated tick host breadth because rare associations were frequently missed under finite field sampling.





Under equal exhaustive sampling, all 13 tick species were predicted to infest 34–37 of the 37 available host species.





Host-specificity indices derived directly from observed interaction counts created spurious differences among tick species that largely disappeared after accounting for sampling uncertainty.





Multi-level Bayesian models can infer species-level ecological network properties from individual-level observations while incorporating zero encounters, covariates and uncertainty.





Ecological network analyses based only on aggregated adjacency matrices risk overestimating specialisation when species are unevenly sampled.





Host availability, abundance and space use are likely to be more important determinants of tick survival and reproduction than rigid host specialisation in this Bornean system.





Comparative network studies should retain disaggregated individual-level observations so that differences in sampling intensity and false zero interactions can be modelled explicitly.

Shifts from native to invasive small mammals across gradients from tropical forest to urban habitat in Borneo


Konstans Wells, Maklarin B. Lakim, Robert B. O’Hara


Full citation

Wells, K., Lakim, M. B., & O’Hara, R. B. (2014). Shifts from native to invasive small mammals across gradients from tropical forest to urban habitat in Borneo. Biodiversity and Conservation, 23(9), 2289-2303. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10531-014-0723-5

Modelled occurrence probabilities of four common small mammal taxa across increasing land-use intensity in Kota Kinabalu. Müller’s sundamys declined steadily from forest to urban habitat, Asian black rats and Asian house shrews peaked at intermediate land-use intensity, and Norway rats increased towards the most urbanised habitats. The contrasting responses illustrate a transition from native to invasive and commensal small mammal assemblages. Credit: Wells, Lakim and O’Hara (2014)




Research overview


The study demonstrates a marked turnover from native forest small mammals to invasive and commensal species across a tropical urbanisation gradient. Native Müller’s sundamys persisted only where vegetation remained, while Asian black rats and Asian house shrews were favoured by intermediate disturbance and Norway rats by intensive urbanisation. The work links biodiversity loss, biological invasion and potential disease transmission across forest–urban interfaces.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Native small mammal communities in the Kota Kinabalu landscape were largely replaced by invasive and commensal species as land-use intensity increased from forest to urban habitat.





Müller’s sundamys was the only common native non-flying small mammal recorded in urban and suburban habitats, and its occurrence probability declined continuously with increasing land-use intensity.





Asian black rats reached their highest occurrence probabilities at intermediate land-use intensity but also occupied highly urbanised habitats and occasionally entered forested habitats.





Asian house shrews were most likely to occur at intermediate land-use intensity and were uncommon in both intact forest and the most intensively urbanised habitat.





Norway rats were restricted primarily to highly urbanised habitats and showed increasing occurrence probability with land-use intensity.





Fine-scale fallow vegetation increased the occurrence probability of Müller’s sundamys and Asian house shrews in urban and suburban landscapes.





Nine additional native small mammal species were recorded only in forested habitats near the urban landscape, indicating strong exclusion from anthropogenic environments.





Species responses to land-use intensity were frequently non-linear, demonstrating the value of polynomial occupancy models for analysing heterogeneous urban–forest gradients.





Müller’s sundamys and Asian black rats may function as ecological links between forest wildlife and urban species because they occur across broad portions of the land-use gradient.





Broad occurrence across forest–urban interfaces may make Müller’s sundamys and Asian black rats important host bridges for parasite and pathogen transmission.





Conservation of near-natural forest within urban and suburban landscapes may help retain native small mammals and constrain the spread of invasive commensal species.





Future studies should combine habitat, species-interaction and molecular-taxonomic data to distinguish environmental filtering from competition and cryptic species turnover within the Rattus rattus complex.

Targeted conservation to safeguard a biodiversity hotspot from climate and land-cover change


Matthew J. Struebig, Andreas Wilting, David L. A. Gaveau, Erik Meijaard, Robert J. Smith, Tajuddin Abdullah, Nicola Abram, Raymond Alfred, Marc Ancrenaz, Dave M. Augeri, Jerrold L. Research overview


The study integrates species-distribution modelling, deforestation projections and minimum-set spatial prioritisation under multiple climate, emission and presence-threshold scenarios. Combined environmental change was projected to cause major habitat contraction and upslope shifts for many primates, carnivores and bats. Priority-area analyses consistently emphasised Borneo's interior uplands, connectivity among reserves and land managed under forestry rather than protection confined to the existing reserve network.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Under combined climate and land-cover change projections, 30%–49% of the 81 modelled Bornean mammal species could lose at least 30% of suitable habitat by 2080.





Suitable ecological conditions were projected to shift upslope for 23%–46% of Bornean mammal species by 2080, with particularly strong implications for carnivores and primates.





Corrected calculations indicate that at least 14 carnivore, four primate and 11 bat species could face heightened extinction risk by 2080.





Existing mid- and high-elevation protected areas may represent an increasing proportion of suitable habitat if species can colonise newly suitable upland areas under climate change.





Conservation planning across present, 2050 and 2080 conditions requires additional land outside the existing reserve network, including connections among fragmented reserves and protection of lowland habitat.





Treating forestry reserves as part of the conservation estate could meet most mammal representation targets with approximately 16,000–28,000 km² of additional priority land.





A large share of priority areas lies under forestry jurisdiction, identifying logging and plantation sectors as essential partners for climate-smart biodiversity conservation on Borneo.





Conservation partnerships in production forests should combine improved forestry practices, hunting control, road closure and maintenance of forest corridors between lowland and upland reserves.

title: Timing and severity of immunizing diseases in rabbits is controlled by seasonal matching of host and pathogen dynamics
text:
Research article

Timing and severity of immunizing diseases in rabbits is controlled by seasonal matching of host and pathogen dynamics


Konstans Wells, Barry W. Brook, Robert C. Lacy, Greg J. Mutze, David E. Peacock, Ron G. Sinclair, Nina Schwensow, Phillip Cassey, Robert B. O’Hara, Damien A. Fordham


Full citation

Wells, K., Brook, B. W., Lacy, R. C., Mutze, G. J., Peacock, D. E., Sinclair, R. G., Schwensow, N., Cassey, P., O’Hara, R. B., & Fordham, D. A. (2015). Timing and severity of immunizing diseases in rabbits is controlled by seasonal matching of host and pathogen dynamics. Journal of the Royal Society Interface, 12, 20141184. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2014.1184



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The publication shows that disease severity emerges from phenological matching between host recruitment and pathogen activity rather than from pathogen parameters alone. Juvenile insusceptibility and maternal antibodies delay exposure to rabbit haemorrhagic disease, while recovery from myxomatosis alters the pool of hosts available to the second virus. These coupled seasonal processes determine recurrent epidemics and stochastic local-population persistence.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Only models that included seasonal matching between rabbit reproduction and virus introduction reproduced the observed fluctuations in rabbit abundance and recurrent rabbit haemorrhagic disease outbreaks.





At the Turretfield study site, rabbit reproduction peaked around calendar week 37, whereas rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus introduction generally began earlier, around calendar week 30.





Rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus introduction was estimated to persist for approximately 23 weeks annually, indicating that continuous year-round introduction or perpetuation was unlikely at the study site.





Juvenile insusceptibility and maternally derived antibodies were estimated to provide approximately 30 days of full protection against rabbit haemorrhagic disease, making delayed infection an important seasonal mechanism.





Recovery from myxomatosis had the greatest influence on simulated fatalities from rabbit haemorrhagic disease, demonstrating indirect interactions between the two co-circulating immunizing viruses.





Recovery rates from myxomatosis and rabbit haemorrhagic disease were the strongest determinants of simulated local rabbit-population extinction.





Earlier juvenile susceptibility to myxomatosis increased population extinction risk and reduced the pool of juveniles subsequently susceptible to rabbit haemorrhagic disease.





Epidemiological models of immunizing wildlife diseases should explicitly represent seasonal matching among host recruitment, juvenile immunity and pathogen introduction when evaluating disease severity and population viability.

title: Environmental effects and individual body condition drive seasonal fecundity of rabbits: identifying acute and lagged processes
text:
Research article

Environmental effects and individual body condition drive seasonal fecundity of rabbits: identifying acute and lagged processes


Konstans Wells, Robert B. O’Hara, Brian D. Cooke, Greg J. Mutze, Thomas A. A. Prowse, Damien A. Fordham


Full citation

Wells, K., O’Hara, R. B., Cooke, B. D., Mutze, G. J., Prowse, T. A. A., & Fordham, D. A. (2016). Environmental effects and individual body condition drive seasonal fecundity of rabbits: identifying acute and lagged processes. Oecologia, 181(3), 853-864. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00442-016-3617-2



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Seasonal and interannual dynamics of rabbit fecundity. This conceptual framework illustrates how reproductive activity in European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) varies within and among years in response to environmental conditions. Seasonal breeding begins following autumn pasture growth, peaks during the main winter breeding season, and fluctuates between years according to changing resource availability. The framework highlights how lagged environmental effects and reproductive investment in preceding seasons can influence subsequent breeding probabilities and fecundity, providing the conceptual basis for analysing immediate and delayed drivers of reproduction using distributed lag models. The study demonstrates that rabbit fecundity is shaped not only by current rainfall, temperature and body condition, but also by the ecological history of individuals and populations, offering new insights into demographic responses to environmental variability and climate change. Credit: Wells et al. (2016)




Research overview


The study demonstrates that rabbit fecundity emerges from interactions among seasonal climate, individual condition and previous reproductive effort. Rainfall can trigger earlier breeding through effects lasting several weeks, but early reproduction may be offset by reduced later breeding. Body condition strongly determines which females reproduce under marginal or late-season conditions, showing that individual heterogeneity is central to population-level reproductive dynamics.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Rabbit breeding probability was highly seasonal, peaking during July to October and remaining low during the dry summer months.





Summer rainfall increased rabbit breeding probability immediately and through lagged effects lasting up to approximately 10 weeks.





An earlier onset of seasonal breeding did not increase total annual reproductive output because elevated early breeding reduced breeding probability in the subsequent main season.





Better kidney fat condition increased summer breeding probability and embryo survival, particularly when environmental conditions were marginal.





Higher body mass relative to age increased breeding probability during the main and late breeding seasons and increased ovulation rate across most of the breeding period.





Only females in good body condition were likely to continue breeding late in the annual reproductive cycle.





Higher temperatures reduced rabbit breeding probability across most seasons, although the estimated effect was modest.





Rainfall increased ovulation rate during the main breeding season with lagged effects extending to approximately 14 weeks.





Rabbit fecundity was more strongly associated with individual body condition than with direct population-level environmental indices such as pasture growth, soil moisture or density.





Distributed lag models improved inference about breeding probability by estimating the timescale over which environmental exposure affected reproduction.





Seasonal reproductive plasticity can buffer short-term environmental stress without necessarily increasing annual fecundity.





Forecasts of climate effects on highly fecund mammals should model both seasonal shifts in reproduction and delayed environmental effects rather than relying on annual averages.

title: Infection of the fittest: devil facial tumour disease has greatest effect on individuals with highest reproductive output
text:
Research article

Infection of the fittest: devil facial tumour disease has greatest effect on individuals with highest reproductive output


Konstans Wells, Rodrigo K. Hamede, Douglas H. Kerlin, Andrew Storfer, Paul A. Hohenlohe, Menna E. Jones, Hamish I. McCallum


Full citation

Conceptual pathways linking Tasmanian devil survival, reproduction and devil facial tumour disease progression. Scenarios (a–b) illustrate population decline when individuals fail to reproduce or die rapidly after tumour development. Scenarios (c–d) show how infected individuals may still contribute offspring when disease occurs later in life or progresses slowly, while scenario (e) represents repeated reproduction by an uninfected individual. The figure highlights the need to analyse survival, fecundity and disease progression within an integrated demographic and epidemiological framework. Credit: Konstans Wells et al. (2017)




Research overview


The study demonstrates that infection risk is not necessarily greatest among the weakest individuals in a population. Instead, DFTD selectively affects high-fitness, socially dominant Tasmanian devils that contribute disproportionately to population growth. By integrating epidemiological and demographic processes within a unified Bayesian state-space framework, the study links individual disease progression to population-level dynamics and provides a general methodological framework for investigating emerging wildlife diseases. The findings reshape understanding of disease-mediated selection by showing that pathogens can remove the individuals with the greatest reproductive value, thereby altering both population viability and evolutionary trajectories.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Tasmanian devils that eventually develop devil facial tumour disease exhibit higher survival and greater lifetime reproductive output before infection than individuals that never become infected, indicating that the disease disproportionately affects the fittest members of the population.





Increasing tumour burden substantially reduces host survival, although individuals with small tumour loads can retain higher survival probabilities than devils that never become infected.





Female Tasmanian devils that become infected reproduce more frequently during their lifetime and produce larger litters than females that remain uninfected, demonstrating that infection is associated with individuals of high reproductive value.





Integrating disease progression, survival and fecundity within a Bayesian state-space mark–recapture framework enables estimation of individual fitness and disease dynamics throughout the lifetime of hosts.





Wildlife diseases that preferentially infect individuals with the highest reproductive value can have disproportionately large impacts on population dynamics and evolutionary trajectories because they remove the individuals contributing most to future population growth.

title: Unravelling changing interspecific interactions across environmental gradients using Markov random fields
text:
Methods article

Unravelling changing interspecific interactions across environmental gradients using Markov random fields


Nicholas J. Clark, Konstans Wells, Oscar Lindberg


Full citation

Clark, N. J., Wells, K., & Lindberg, O. (2018). Unravelling changing interspecific interactions across environmental gradients using Markov random fields. Ecology, 99(6), 1277-1283. https://doi.org/10.1002/ecy.2221



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Conditional random field predictions of how interactions among mosquito larvae, aquatic predators and other marsh organisms change with increasing water temperature. Network edges represent conditional associations after accounting for the remaining species and environmental covariates. Positive interactions are shown in red, negative interactions in blue, and line thickness indicates interaction strength. The sequence demonstrates that both the direction and magnitude of ecological associations can vary across environmental gradients. Credit: Clark, Wells and Lindberg (2018)




Research overview


The study presents Markov random fields as graphical network models that distinguish direct conditional dependencies from associations generated indirectly through other species. By adding covariates, conditional random fields estimate how interaction coefficients change with environmental conditions and allow their effect sizes to be compared directly with abiotic predictors. Case studies show that parasite co-infections vary with host abundance and that mosquito–predator associations shift with water temperature and other habitat gradients. The accompanying MRFcov R package makes the framework accessible for applied ecological analyses.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Markov random fields can estimate direct conditional dependencies among species from multispecies presence–absence data while controlling for indirect associations mediated through other species.





Conditional random fields extend Markov random fields by incorporating environmental covariates, allowing the direction and strength of interspecific associations to vary across environmental gradients.





In avian blood-parasite communities, Plasmodium and microfilaria showed a positive conditional association, whereas the two focal Haemoproteus complexes showed a strong negative association.





Associations between both Haemoproteus complexes and Plasmodium became more positive as the relative abundance of Zosterops hosts increased, while the association between Haemoproteus zosteropis and microfilaria became more negative.





Interspecific parasite associations were stronger predictors of Haemoproteus zosteropis occurrence than host relative abundance, demonstrating that conditional random fields permit direct comparison between biotic and environmental effect sizes.





Culex modestus and Culex pipiens showed a strong positive association, consistent with shared larval habitat requirements.





Negative associations between predatory aquatic insects and mosquito larvae changed across water-temperature gradients, indicating that potential predator effects are environmentally context dependent.





L1 regularisation and cross-validation enable conditional random fields to estimate sparse ecological interaction networks while reducing overfitting in datasets containing many species and covariates.





Conditional random fields provide a complementary approach to joint species distribution models when the research objective is to identify interpretable, environmentally varying conditional associations among species.





The MRFcov R package provides tools for fitting, visualising and interpreting Markov and conditional random fields for ecological presence–absence data.

title: Global spread of helminth parasites at the human–domestic animal–wildlife interface
text:
Research article

Global spread of helminth parasites at the human–domestic animal–wildlife interface


Konstans Wells, David I. Gibson, Nicholas J. Clark, Alexis Ribas, Serge Morand, Hamish I. McCallum


Full citation

Wells, K., Gibson, D. I., Clark, N. J., Ribas, A., Morand, S., & McCallum, H. I. (2018). Global spread of helminth parasites at the human–domestic animal–wildlife interface. Global Change Biology, 24(7), 3254–3265. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.14064



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Bipartite network of the most geographically widespread helminth parasites and their associations with wildlife species pools across the world's zoogeographical regions. Upper nodes represent zoogeographical regions and lower nodes represent parasite species. Link widths are proportional to the fraction of sampled wildlife species in each region associated with a given parasite. Parasite node colours indicate the number of focal domestic host species (humans, dogs, cats, cattle, pigs, black rats and brown rats) that also host each parasite. Widespread parasites, identified using the highest Shannon diversity index values (n = 31), are predominantly shared among multiple domestic host species, highlighting the broad connectivity of helminth transmission across wildlife, domestic animals and humans. The Madagascan region is omitted because none of the displayed parasite species were recorded from sampled wildlife there. Credit: Konstans Wells




Research overview


The study identifies trophic ecology as a major organising mechanism of helminth sharing at the human–domestic animal–wildlife interface. Wildlife diet class consistently outweighed most climatic, habitat and life-history predictors, while geographical projections showed correlated risk patterns across humans, dogs, cats, livestock and commensal rats. The results connect host traits, multispecies trophic interactions, biogeography and parasite host shifting within a global One Health framework, while emphasising that uneven sampling and presence-only records constrain precise local prediction.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Wildlife diet class was the strongest predictor of helminth parasite sharing with humans and focal domestic mammals across the analysed parasite groups and host species.





Diet class explained substantially more variation in wildlife helminth association risk than zoogeographical region, host habitat, climatic niche or most other evaluated traits.





Herbivorous and carnivorous wildlife generally had higher predicted risks of sharing helminths with humans and domestic animals than insectivorous wildlife.





Forty-one per cent of the 1,345 mammalian wildlife species in the host–parasite database were recorded with helminth species also found in humans.





Of the 397 helminth species recorded from humans, 195 were also recorded from wildlife and 182 from at least one other domestic host.





Predicted wildlife association risks were strongly correlated across several human and domestic host comparisons, indicating broadly similar geographical patterns of helminth sharing among focal hosts.





Wildlife in the Nearctic and Palaearctic regions showed comparatively high predicted risks of sharing helminths with humans across nematodes, cestodes and trematodes.





The most geographically widespread helminths were commonly associated with multiple domestic host species as well as wildlife.





Helminth transmission at the human–wildlife interface cannot be understood independently of domestic animals because multiple domestic hosts participate in overlapping parasite-sharing patterns.





Future range shifts and novel trophic interactions may create new pathways for helminth host shifting among wildlife, domestic animals and humans.





Predictive assessments of zoonotic helminth risk should incorporate multispecies trophic networks rather than relying only on local wildlife species richness.





Presence-only host–parasite records, incomplete parasite inventories, uneven sampling effort and uncertain local interaction conditions limit the precision of the projected association risks.

Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study provides a global test of the extinction-filter hypothesis by linking contemporary animal responses to forest edges with long-term exposure to fire, glaciation, tropical storms and historical forest loss. Communities in frequently disturbed regions contained fewer forest-core and edge-avoiding species, consistent with past local extinction or evolutionary adaptation filtering out sensitive taxa. This historical contingency helps reconcile divergent conclusions about fragmentation effects across regions and taxa.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Across 73 datasets containing 4,489 animal species, the proportion of fragmentation-sensitive forest species was nearly three times higher in regions with low historical disturbance than in regions with high historical disturbance.





Historical exposure to severe disturbances was associated with a 79% reduction in the odds that a forest species was classified as a forest-core species.





Forest-edge avoidance was more prevalent in low-disturbance regions, where 51.3% of forest species avoided edges, than in high-disturbance regions, where 18.1% avoided edges.





Fragmentation sensitivity declined strongly with latitude, consistent with tropical species having experienced less historical disturbance and therefore retaining greater sensitivity to forest edges.





Historical natural and anthropogenic disturbances appear to act as extinction filters by removing disturbance-sensitive species or favouring adaptation among species that persist in repeatedly disturbed regions.





Conservation measures that reduce edge creation and forest fragmentation should be prioritised in historically low-disturbance regions, particularly tropical forests and biodiversity hotspots.





Regional disturbance history helps explain why studies have reported widely variable effects of habitat fragmentation across taxa and geographical regions.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Habitat loss is the primary driver of biodiversity decline worldwide, but the effects of fragmentation (i.e., the spatial arrangement of remaining habitat) are debated. We tested the hypothesis that forest fragmentation sensitivity—affected by avoidance of habitat edges—should be driven by historical exposure, and therefore species’ evolutionary responses, to disturbance. Using a database containing 73 datasets worldwide (4,489 animal species), we found that the proportion of fragmentation-sensitive species was nearly three times higher in regions with low versus high rates of historical disturbance (i.e., fires, glaciation, hurricanes, and deforestation). These disturbances coincide with a latitudinal gradient in which sensitivity increases six-fold at low versus high latitudes. We conclude that conservation efforts to limit edges created by fragmentation will be most important in the world’s tropical forests.

It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study shows that bat paramyxovirus communities exhibit strongly clustered, multi-virus shedding dynamics. Although average prevalence was low, nine viruses were detected and several coalesced into an intense winter 2011 shedding pulse that coincided with unprecedented Hendra virus spillover. Conditional association models revealed both positive and negative virus-pair patterns, while comparisons across sample and roost session levels provided hypotheses about facilitation, cross-immunity, co-infection and shared environmental forcing.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Australian flying-fox populations commonly shed multiple paramyxoviruses, with nine viral species detected across 1,131 pooled under-roost urine samples.





Multi-virus shedding occasionally formed an extreme, brief and spatially restricted pulse that coincided with the exceptional winter 2011 peak in Hendra virus spillover to horses.





Viral detections were strongly clustered in space and time, with most paramyxoviruses occurring at low average prevalence but appearing synchronously during short shedding pulses.





Up to six paramyxoviruses were detected in a single pooled urine sample during the winter 2011 shedding pulse at Boonah.





Markov random field analyses identified predominantly positive conditional associations among bat paramyxoviruses, consistent with shared environmental drivers or facilitative interactions.





Teviot paramyxovirus showed the strongest and most consistently positive sample-level associations with other viruses, suggesting a central role in multi-virus co-detection.





Hendra virus and Yeppoon paramyxovirus were strongly negatively associated at the sample level, a pattern consistent with competition, cross-immunity or host-specific segregation.





Differences between sample-level and session-level associations can help distinguish likely within-host co-infection from population-level co-circulation driven by shared temporal or environmental conditions.





Detection of several paramyxoviruses was associated with dry winter conditions and with the relative abundance of black and grey-headed flying foxes.





Routine surveillance with short study duration or infrequent sampling can miss intense multi-virus shedding pulses and thereby underestimate their contribution to zoonotic spillover risk.





Longitudinal surveillance at intervals of approximately one to two months over at least two years is required to improve detection of temporally concentrated viral shedding events in flying-fox populations.





Predicting bat-borne virus spillover requires an ecological community perspective that integrates host ecology, environmental change and interactions among multiple viruses rather than focusing on single pathogens.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Within host-parasite communities, viral co-circulation and co-infections of hosts are the norm, yet studies of significant emerging zoonoses tend to focus on a single parasite species within the host. Using a multiplexed paramyxovirus bead-based PCR on urine samples from Australian flying foxes, we show that multi-viral shedding from flying fox populations is common. We detected up to nine bat paramyxoviruses shed synchronously. Multi-viral shedding infrequently coalesced into an extreme, brief and spatially restricted shedding pulse, coinciding with peak spillover of Hendra virus, an emerging fatal zoonotic pathogen of high interest. Such extreme pulses of multi-viral shedding could easily be missed during routine surveillance yet have potentially serious consequences for spillover of novel pathogens to humans and domestic animal hosts. We also detected co-occurrence patterns suggestive of the presence of interactions among viruses, such as facilitation and cross-immunity. We propose that multiple viruses may be interacting, influencing the shedding and spillover of zoonotic pathogens. Understanding these interactions in the context of broader scale drivers, such as habitat loss, may help predict shedding pulses of Hendra virus and other fatal zoonoses.

title: Global patterns in helminth host specificity: phylogenetic and functional diversity of regional host species pools matter
text:
Research article

Global patterns in helminth host specificity: phylogenetic and functional diversity of regional host species pools matter


Konstans Wells, David I. Gibson, Nicholas J. Clark


Full citation

Wells, K., Gibson, D. I., & Clark, N. J. (2019). Global patterns in helminth host specificity: phylogenetic and functional diversity of regional host species pools matter. Ecography, 42(3), 416-427. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.03886



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The study demonstrates that parasite host specificity is not a fixed species-level property but a realised outcome shaped by regional host community composition. Phylogenetic and functional host breadth varied substantially among parasites and regions, with some helminths restricted to related or ecologically similar hosts and others able to infect hosts spanning diverse ecological niches. By explicitly accounting for available prospective hosts, the analytical framework provides a more comparable measure of host specificity and host-shifting potential across biogeographical settings.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Realised phylogenetic and functional host specificity of globally widespread helminth parasites varies among zoogeographical regions because the composition and diversity of prospective mammalian host pools differ geographically.





Helminth parasites generally exhibited the lowest phylogenetic host specificity in the Neotropical, Saharo-Arabian and Australian regions, where prospective host pools contained the greatest variation in mammalian phylogenetic diversity.





Hydatigera taeniaeformis and Hymenolepis diminuta infected mammalian host assemblages that were less phylogenetically diverse than expected from regional species pools, indicating constrained host shifting into distantly related hosts.





Echinococcus granulosus, Mesocestoides lineatus and Trichinella spiralis infected host assemblages that were less functionally diverse than expected, suggesting that host shifts tend to occur among mammals occupying similar ecological niches.





Hydatigera taeniaeformis infected a greater functional diversity of mammalian hosts than expected, indicating substantial capacity to shift among hosts with different ecological characteristics.





Mammalian host traits provided limited prediction of helminth association probability after accounting for host phylogeny, demonstrating that phylogenetic relationships remain a major determinant of observed host–parasite associations.





Assessments of parasite host specificity and invasion potential should compare observed infected-host diversity with the phylogenetic and functional diversity available in the relevant regional host species pool.





Domestic and commensal mammals, including dogs, cats and Rattus species, may facilitate the global spread of helminths by connecting parasite transmission cycles with diverse endemic wildlife communities.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Host specificity has a major influence on a parasite’s ability to shift between human and animal host species. Yet there is a dearth of quantitative approaches to explore variation in host specificity across biogeographical scales, particularly in response to the varying community compositions of potential hosts. We built a global dataset of intermediate host associations for nine of the world’s most widespread helminth parasites (all of which infect humans). Using hierarchical models, we asked if realised parasite host specificity varied in response to regional variation in the phylogenetic and functional diversities of potential host species. Parasites were recorded in 4–10 zoogeographical regions, with some showing considerable geographical variation in observed versus expected host specificity. Parasites generally exhibited the lowest phylogenetic host specificity in regions with the greatest variation in prospective host phylogenetic diversity, namely the Neotropical, Saharo-Arabian and Australian regions. Globally, we uncovered notable variation in parasite host shifting potential. Observed host assemblages for Hydatigera taeniaeformis and Hymenolepis diminuta were less phylogenetically diverse than expected, suggesting limited potential to spillover into unrelated hosts. Host assemblages for Echinococcus granulosus, Mesocestoides lineatus and Trichinella spiralis were less functionally diverse than expected, suggesting limited potential to shift across host ecological niches. By contrast, Hydatigera taeniaeformis infected a higher functional diversity of hosts than expected, indicating strong potential to shift across hosts with different ecological niches. We show that the realised phylogenetic and functional diversities of infected hosts are determined by biogeographical gradients in prospective host species pools. These findings emphasise the need to account for underlying species diversity when assessing parasite host specificity. Our framework to identify variation in realised host specificity is broadly applicable to other host–parasite systems and will provide key insights into parasite invasion potential at regional and global scales.

title: Disease control across urban–rural gradients
text:
Research article

Disease control across urban–rural gradients


Konstans Wells, Miguel Lurgi, Brendan Collins, Biagio Lucini, Rowland R. Kao, Alun L. Lloyd, Simon D. W. Frost, Mike B. Gravenor


Full citation

Wells, K., Lurgi, M., Collins, B., Lucini, B., Kao, R. R., Lloyd, A. L., Frost, S. D. W., & Gravenor, M. B. (2020). Disease control across urban–rural gradients. Journal of the Royal Society Interface, 17, 20200775. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2020.0775



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.




Conceptual framework for SARS-CoV-2 spread and control across an urban–rural metapopulation. Epidemiological transitions are represented with a stochastic susceptible–exposed–asymptomatic–infectious–removed model. Connected rural and urban populations exchange commuter travellers, creating changing source–sink dynamics as outbreaks alter local pools of susceptible individuals. The lower panels compare isolation of all infected people, isolation of symptomatic cases only, and regional lockdowns that reduce local transmission and travel. Credit: Wells et al. (2020)




Research overview


The study links individual infection dynamics with population connectivity, commuting and spatial variation in urban and rural communities. It shows that intervention efficacy depends strongly on the background transmission rate and on whether non-symptomatic infections are detected. Symptom-based isolation and reactive regional lockdowns usually provide limited control, whereas tracing and isolating infected individuals across exposed, asymptomatic and symptomatic states can greatly suppress epidemic size. The analysis also introduces an urban–rural epidemic gradient to quantify how regional outbreak size changes with population connectivity.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Isolation of symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 cases alone has limited capacity to reduce total epidemic size unless the overall transmission rate remains persistently low.





Regional lockdowns triggered by local outbreaks have limited long-term efficacy when transmission rates are high and are most effective when introduced at low outbreak thresholds.





Detecting and isolating non-symptomatic infected individuals through effective testing and contact tracing substantially reduces epidemic size across a wider range of transmission conditions than symptom-based isolation.





In the simulations, isolating at least 47% of all infected individuals reduced epidemic size to less than 5% of the corresponding uncontrolled scenario.





Urban–rural gradients in epidemic size arise because highly connected urban populations can experience larger outbreaks than less connected rural populations.





Higher commuter travel frequencies strengthen urban–rural differences in epidemic size under regional lockdown strategies, indicating reduced lockdown efficacy in highly connected urban populations.





High transmission rates produce the strongest urban–rural gradients when all infected individuals are isolated or regional lockdowns are used, whereas symptom-only isolation produces the opposite pattern.





Maintaining low background transmission is more important for limiting total epidemic size than repeatedly adjusting short-term regional control measures in response to observed case numbers.





Strategic individual-based metapopulation models can reveal how intervention efficacy depends on interactions among transmission, mobility, population connectivity and spatial variation in susceptibility.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Controlling the regional re-emergence of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) after its initial spread in ever-changing personal contact networks and disease landscapes is a challenging task. In a landscape context, contact opportunities within and between populations are changing rapidly as lockdown measures are relaxed and a number of social activities re-activated. Using an individual-based metapopulation model, we explored the efficacy of different control strategies across an urban–rural gradient in Wales, UK. Our model shows that isolation of symptomatic cases or regional lockdowns in response to local outbreaks have limited efficacy unless the overall transmission rate is kept persistently low. Additional isolation of non-symptomatic infected individuals, who may be detected by effective test-and-trace strategies, is pivotal to reducing the overall epidemic size over a wider range of transmission scenarios. We define an ‘urban–rural gradient in epidemic size’ as a correlation between regional epidemic size and connectivity within the region, with more highly connected urban populations experiencing relatively larger outbreaks. For interventions focused on regional lockdowns, the strength of such gradients in epidemic size increased with higher travel frequencies, indicating a reduced efficacy of the control measure in the urban regions under these conditions. When both non-symptomatic and symptomatic individuals are isolated or regional lockdown strategies are enforced, we further found the strongest urban–rural epidemic gradients at high transmission rates. This effect was reversed for strategies targeted at symptomatic individuals only. Our results emphasize the importance of test-and-trace strategies and maintaining low transmission rates for efficiently controlling SARS-CoV-2 spread, both at landscape scale and in urban areas.

Regional and spatial variation in avian haemosporidian infection probability. Realm-level estimates compare average prevalence of four parasite genera among ten zoogeographical regions using 53,669 sampled birds. Global maps show location-specific posterior mean prevalence where estimates had sufficiently low uncertainty, revealing local hotspots that are not confined to the regions with the highest overall prevalence. Credit: Fecchio et al. (2021)




Research overview


The study demonstrates that drivers of avian haemosporidian infection are strongly context dependent across parasite genera and zoogeographical regions. Host traits such as migration distance, body mass and canopy foraging frequently varied in effect among realms, whereas climatic effects were comparatively more consistent. Infection hotspots also occurred within otherwise low-prevalence regions, indicating that local habitat and microclimate interact with global drivers. The work establishes a spatio-phylogenetic hierarchical framework for separating global average effects from region-specific deviations.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Infection probabilities of avian haemosporidian parasites vary substantially among zoogeographical realms and among avian host families.





Leucocytozoon, Parahaemoproteus and Plasmodium reached their highest estimated realm-level infection probabilities in the Saharo-Arabian region.





Host ecological traits often had different or opposite effects on haemosporidian infection probability among zoogeographical realms, whereas climatic effects were generally more consistent across regions.





Migration distance increased Parahaemoproteus and Plasmodium infection probability in some realms but decreased infection probability in others, demonstrating strong regional context dependence.





Local bird species richness increased Leucocytozoon and Parahaemoproteus infection probability at the global scale, but the effect of richness on Parahaemoproteus varied in direction among realms.





Larger host body mass was associated with increased infection probability for Leucocytozoon, Parahaemoproteus and Plasmodium.





Wetland cover increased Plasmodium infection probability but decreased Leucocytozoon and Parahaemoproteus infection probability, indicating parasite-genus-specific environmental responses.





Distance from the equator and annual mean temperature showed no consistent global association with infection probability for the three most prevalent haemosporidian genera.





Some low-prevalence zoogeographical realms contained pronounced local infection hotspots, showing that regional habitat and microclimatic variation can generate transmission patterns not captured by realm-level averages.





Models combining spatial effects, host phylogenetic structure and region-specific varying coefficients provided the strongest fit and predictive performance for global avian haemosporidian infection data.





Predicting future changes in avian haemosporidian infection risk requires simultaneous consideration of landscape conditions, climate, host traits, host community assembly and regional variation in their effects.

title: Challenges in modeling the emergence of novel pathogens
text:
Review

Challenges in modeling the emergence of novel pathogens


Emma E. Glennon, Marjolein Bruijning, Justin Lessler, Ian F. Miller, Benjamin L. Rice, Robin N. Thompson, Konstans Wells, C. Jessica E. Metcalf


Full citation

Glennon, E. E., Bruijning, M., Lessler, J., Miller, I. F., Rice, B. L., Thompson, R. N., Wells, K., & Metcalf, C. J. E. (2021). Challenges in modeling the emergence of novel pathogens. Epidemics, 37, 100516. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.epidem.2021.100516



Publisher article



About this knowledge page. This BAHE Research Record provides curated notes and links for the peer-reviewed publication. It supports discovery and interpretation but does not replace the publisher-hosted version of record, which remains the authoritative scientific source and should be cited as the primary reference.



Research overview


The paper frames pathogen emergence as a multi-stage process involving introduction into a new host population and subsequent establishment of sustained transmission. It connects surveillance design, pathogen and host traits, immune landscapes, evolutionary change, within-host processes, population heterogeneity, parameter estimation and health-system capacity. The review also treats modelling as a social and institutional practice: data biases, structural inequalities, communication failures and unequal access to analytical capacity can shape both scientific inference and public health outcomes.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Pathogen emergence in a new host population comprises dynamically distinct processes of introduction and establishment that require different data and modelling approaches.





Mathematical models can identify the temporal, spatial and sampling designs needed for surveillance systems to detect novel pathogens and emerging variants before widespread transmission occurs.





Available emergence data are systematically biased toward larger, clinically distinctive outbreaks occurring in places with stronger diagnostic and surveillance capacity.





Predicting zoonotic emergence requires linking pathogen and host traits with fine-scale species distributions, exposure processes, environmental change and the immune landscape of potential host populations.





Genotype-to-phenotype relationships, within-host dynamics and cross-reactive immunity remain major unresolved components of models seeking to anticipate pathogen host range, adaptation and pandemic potential.





Early estimates of reproductive numbers, incubation periods, asymptomatic infection and establishment risk are highly uncertain and must be interpreted in relation to transmission heterogeneity and local epidemiological context.





Integrating genomic, serological, mobility, clinical and ecological data can strengthen inference about emerging epidemics, but sampling bias and model misspecification must be explicitly represented.





Complex mechanistic models of disease emergence must balance realistic social, spatial and biological structure against parameter uncertainty, computational tractability and limited empirical evidence.





Effective public-health modelling requires transparent communication of assumptions, uncertainty and changing evidence while avoiding overconfident forecasts during the earliest stages of an outbreak.





Equitable pandemic preparedness depends on sustained collaboration among modellers, public-health practitioners and affected communities, together with accessible tools, shared data infrastructure and recognition of structural inequalities shaping disease risk.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


The emergence of infectious agents with pandemic potential present scientific challenges from detection to data interpretation to understanding determinants of risk and forecasts. Mathematical models could play an essential role in how we prepare for future emergent pathogens. Here, we describe core directions for expansion of the existing tools and knowledge base, including: using mathematical models to identify critical directions and paths for strengthening data collection to detect and respond to outbreaks of novel pathogens; expanding basic theory to identify infectious agents and contexts that present the greatest risks, over both the short and longer term; by strengthening estimation tools that make the most use of the likely range and uncertainties in existing data; and by ensuring modelling applications are carefully communicated and developed within diverse and equitable collaborations for increased public health benefit.

Research overview


The study advances ecological forecasting by demonstrating that nonlinear ecological processes and temporal dynamics can be modelled simultaneously within a unified probabilistic framework. By integrating hierarchical smooth functions with latent dynamic processes, DGAMs provide more accurate forecasts, improved uncertainty quantification and greater flexibility for analysing complex ecological time series than conventional generalised additive models.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.

Dynamic Generalised Additive Models (DGAMs) integrate nonlinear ecological relationships with latent temporal processes within a unified Bayesian framework, enabling simultaneous inference and forecasting for discrete ecological time series.





Explicitly modelling latent temporal dynamics produces more robust and realistic ecological forecasts than extrapolating smooth functions beyond the range of observed data using conventional Generalised Additive Models.





Hierarchical dynamic factor models provide an efficient approach for forecasting multiple ecological time series by representing shared temporal dynamics through a reduced set of latent processes.





Bayesian probabilistic inference enables ecological forecasts to quantify uncertainty arising from nonlinear predictor effects, latent ecological dynamics and observation processes within a single coherent modelling framework.





Ecological forecasting models should accommodate incomplete observations, irregular sampling and discrete response distributions because these are fundamental characteristics of ecological time-series data rather than exceptional cases.





Reliable ecological forecasting requires integrating mechanistic ecological knowledge with dynamic statistical models that represent both biological processes and their associated uncertainties through time.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Generalised additive models (GAMs) are powerful tools for modelling nonlinear ecological relationships but often perform poorly for forecasting because smooth functions extrapolate unrealistically beyond observed data. This paper introduces Dynamic Generalised Additive Models (DGAMs), which augment GAMs with latent dynamic processes to jointly model nonlinear predictor effects and temporal dependence. The framework is implemented in the open-source R package mvgam and supports Bayesian estimation of hierarchical smooth functions, dynamic latent factors and probabilistic forecasts for discrete ecological time series. Simulation studies and empirical applications demonstrate improved forecasting accuracy and uncertainty quantification relative to conventional GAMs.

Research overview


The study substantially expands known mammalian diversity in ADH7, a gene involved in first-pass ethanol metabolism. It identifies extensive variation at substrate-binding site 294, especially in bats, and infers an ancestral duplication of ADH7 in Chiroptera. Although several variants may alter ethanol affinity, phylogenetically controlled models did not support a simple overarching relationship between fruit or nectar consumption and ADH7 functionality or site-294 substitution.





Knowledge statements


Interpretive statements that distil key ideas and propositions from the publication to support scholarly reflection and discussion. They should be read alongside the complete peer-reviewed article rather than as standalone conclusions.


Knowledge statements are interpretive discussion points derived from the publication. They are intended to support exploration, comparison, and scholarly dialogue across the BAHE knowledge base. Individual statements are intentionally concise and should not be interpreted independently of the complete peer-reviewed publication, which remains the authoritative source for the authors arguments, evidence, and conclusions.






Comparative analyses of ADH7 included 171 mammal species across seven orders, including newly generated sequence data for 59 species.





Most sampled mammals retained alanine at amino-acid site 294 of ADH7, supporting alanine as the ancestral mammalian state at this functionally important substrate-binding position.





Bats showed especially extensive amino-acid variation at site 294, and comparative genome evidence supported an ADH7 duplication in the ancestor of extant bats.





Frugivorous and nectarivorous bats exhibited diverse residues at site 294 with potential consequences for ethanol affinity, whereas comparable variation was limited among insectivorous bats.





Probable ADH7 pseudogenization and gene loss occurred repeatedly across mammalian lineages, including several species with low fruit or nectar consumption.





Phylogenetic generalized linear models found no consistent significant relationship between dietary fruit or nectar consumption and either substitutions at site 294 or retention of a putatively functional ADH7.





The absence of a broad diet association indicates that ADH7 evolution is shaped by more complex lineage-specific, functional and ecological factors than dietary category alone.





Functional assays of newly identified amino-acid variants and broader analyses of complete coding sequences and dietary ethanol exposure are required to determine their adaptive significance.






Original abstract


Abstract from the peer-reviewed publication.


Dietary variation within and across species drives the eco-evolutionary responsiveness of genes necessary to metabolize nutrients and other components. Recent evidence from humans and other mammals suggests that sugar-rich diets of floral nectar and ripe fruit have favoured mutations in, and functional preservation of, the ADH7 gene, which encodes the ADH class 4 enzyme responsible for metabolizing ethanol. Here we interrogate a large, comparative dataset of ADH7 gene sequence variation, including that underlying the amino acid residue located at the key site (294) that regulates the affinity of ADH7 for ethanol. Our analyses span 171 mammal species, including 59 newly sequenced. We report extensive variation, especially among frugivorous and nectarivorous bats, with potential for functional impact. We also report widespread variation in the retention and probable pseudogenization of ADH7. However, we find little statistical evidence of an overarching impact of dietary behaviour on putative ADH7 function or presence of derived alleles at site 294 across mammals, which suggests that the evolution of ADH7 is shaped by complex factors. Our study reports extensive new diversity in a gene of longstanding ecological interest, offers new sources of variation to be explored in functional assays in future study, and advances our understanding of the processes of molecular evolution.

title: The day after mowing: time and type of mowing influence grassland arthropods

Research article

The day after mowing: time and type of mowing influence grassland arthropods


Johanna L. Berger, Michael Staab, Margarita Hartlieb, Nadja K. Simons, Konstans Wells, Martin M. Gossner, Juliane Vogt, Rafael Achury, Sebastian Seibold, Andreas Hemp, Wolfgang W. Weisser, Nico Blüthgen


Full citation

Berger, J. L., Staab, M., Hartlieb, M., Simons, N. K., Wells, K., Gossner, M. M., Vogt, J., Achury, R., Seibold, S., Hemp, A., Weisser, W. W., & Blüthgen, N. (2024).
